entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of addition
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; additionally, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Additionally, [independent clause]. · [Subject], additionally, [predicate]. · [Subject] [verb phrase] and, additionally, [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses; comma after it in front position, commas on both sides in the middle. A comma alone before it is a comma splice.
entries.meaning: Adds one more item to a list of points, and lives mostly in reports, memos, and academic prose. It is the driest of the additive connectors: moreover claims the new point is weightier and besides claims it settles the question, while additionally simply says "and one more thing."
examples: The lease covers utilities; additionally, the landlord pays for trash pickup.
Additionally, we recommend replacing the smoke detectors on the second floor.
Enrollment fell six percent. Additionally, three instructors resigned mid-semester.
The grant funds two positions and, additionally, covers travel to the annual conference.
Applicants must submit transcripts; additionally, two letters of recommendation are required.
The lease, additionally, forbids subletting for the first year.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of addition (one more point of the same kind). Also an ordinary time adverb meaning "once more" (play it again), which sits in the predicate and takes no commas.
entries.pattern: Again, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; again, [independent clause]. · [Subject], again, [predicate]. · [Subject] [verb phrase] again. (time adverb — "once more," no commas)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle; a semicolon or period before it when two independent clauses are involved — a bare comma there is a comma splice. The commas are also what separate the two words: Again, the vote failed ("here is one more point") versus The vote failed again ("a second time").
entries.meaning: The additive again introduces one more instance of the same point rather than the repetition of an event — the "and here's another" of argument, lecture, and testimony. Position and commas do all the work, since stranded at the end of a predicate the same word is the ordinary adverb meaning "a second time."
examples: Again, the department had no written policy on any of this.
The first draft ignored the budget; again, so did the second.
Consider Ohio. Again, the pattern holds: turnout rose in every county that added a polling place.
Her testimony, again, was never challenged by either side.
Again, I want to be clear that nobody has been accused of anything.
He read the paragraph again before signing it. (time adverb — "once more," not a connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of addition
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; [subject] also [verb phrase]. · [Subject] [auxiliary] also [main verb]. · [Subject] [be] also [complement]. · Also, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: A semicolon or period before the clause it sits in, because also joins nothing itself — The clinic is closed Sundays, it also closes early on Fridays is a comma splice. Inside the clause it takes no commas at all: right after the auxiliary or be, or immediately before a one-word main verb. Comma after it only when it opens a sentence.
entries.meaning: The everyday additive adverb, and the one learners most often try to use as a conjunction. And joins; also joins nothing — it simply marks the clause it sits in as an addition to the one before it. Opening a sentence with Also is standard in speech and general writing, though conservative editors prefer In addition in formal prose.
examples: She speaks Portuguese, and she also reads Latin.
The clinic is closed Sundays; it also closes early on Fridays.
Also, don't forget to sign the last page.
We're out of eggs. Also, the milk went bad.
He also mentioned that the deadline had moved to the fifteenth.
The apartment is cheap. It's also the only one with a dishwasher.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of addition (clinching reason). Also a preposition meaning "in addition to" or "apart from," which takes a noun phrase instead of a clause.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. Besides, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; besides, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], and besides, [independent clause]. · Besides [noun phrase], [independent clause]. (preposition)
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it, comma after it — a bare comma between the two clauses is a comma splice. As a preposition it takes no semicolon and no comma of its own, only the comma that closes a fronted phrase: Besides Dan, nobody came.
variants: besides [noun phrase] (the prepositional form: besides the cost)
entries.meaning: Adds the reason the speaker was saving: the clincher meant to end the discussion. It covers the same additive ground as moreover but is far more conversational, and it usually carries an undertone of "and anyway, that settles it." Beside is a different word — the preposition meaning "next to" — and not a spelling variant of this one.
examples: I don't want to drive four hours. Besides, the tickets are sold out.
The couch won't fit through the door; besides, we can't afford it.
"You should apologize." "For what? Besides, she started it."
It's too late to call him. Besides, he never picks up.
The job pays less, and besides, I'd have to move to Cleveland.
Besides the two of us, nobody knew the combination. (preposition — a noun phrase follows, not a clause)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of addition (a clinching extra reason). Formally a relative which pointing back at the whole clause before it, which is why it can attach across a comma.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause], besides which [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Besides which, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; besides which, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Unlike bare besides, this one tolerates a comma before it, because the which subordinates what follows instead of leaving two independent clauses face to face: The car is twenty years old, besides which it burns oil. A period or semicolon is equally correct and is the safer choice in edited prose; the comma after it is optional and usually dropped.
entries.meaning: Piles one more reason onto the one just given, with the same "and that settles it" force as besides. It belongs to letters, columns, and dialogue rather than to reports, and its relative-pronoun grammar is what lets it hang on the previous clause where besides would demand a full stop.
examples: The apartment is out of our price range, besides which it has no parking.
He never returned the deposit. Besides which, he still has my ladder.
I don't have the time; besides which, I'd be terrible at it.
The report came in three weeks late, besides which two of the tables were mislabeled.
She had already booked the flight, besides which her sister was expecting her.

entries.clause: Independent clause or phrase — adverbial link of addition that stretches the previous claim to a further case
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; for that matter, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. For that matter, [independent clause]. · [noun phrase], or [noun phrase] for that matter, [continuation]. · [Independent clause], and for that matter, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it between two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice unless and carries the join — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle. Tacked onto a noun phrase after or, it takes only the commas that fence that phrase.
entries.meaning: Extends what was just said to a further case the hearer may not have considered, usually a broader or more damning one. Where besides adds a separate reason, for that matter stretches the same point until it covers more ground: He hasn't read the contract — for that matter, neither have I.
examples: I've never met the man; for that matter, I'd never heard his name until Tuesday.
The elevator hasn't worked in a month. For that matter, neither has the buzzer.
She doesn't speak French, or Spanish for that matter.
No one on the committee is an engineer; for that matter, no one there has ever built anything.
The rule was never enforced, and for that matter, it was never printed in the handbook.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of addition
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; furthermore, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Furthermore, [independent clause]. · [Subject], furthermore, [predicate]. · [Subject] [verb phrase] and, furthermore, [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides mid-clause. The comma after it is not optional in edited prose.
variants: further (identical function, a shade lighter: Further, the report omits three sources.)
entries.meaning: Adds another point pushing in the same direction as the last one and signals that the argument is still being built. Where moreover presents its point as the heavier one, furthermore merely continues the accumulation.
examples: The contract was never signed; furthermore, no payment was ever made.
Furthermore, the committee failed to record two of its votes.
The study used a small sample. Furthermore, it excluded everyone over sixty.
She argued that the policy was expensive and, furthermore, that it had never worked anywhere.
Further, the audit found no documentation for eleven thousand dollars in travel.
The estimate is, furthermore, three weeks out of date.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of addition. Also in addition to, a preposition taking a noun phrase.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; in addition, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. In addition, [independent clause]. · [Subject], in addition, [predicate]. · [Subject] [verb phrase] and, in addition, [object]. · In addition to [noun phrase], [independent clause]. (preposition)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle. Do not confuse it with the preposition in addition to, which takes a noun phrase and no semicolon: In addition to the analysts, we hired a designer.
variants: in addition to [noun phrase] (the prepositional form, which cannot take a clause)
entries.meaning: The neutral phrasal additive: acceptable in business writing without the starch of furthermore, and safer in formal prose than a sentence-initial Also. It adds a genuinely separate item rather than an elaboration of the previous one.
examples: The apartment includes parking; in addition, the building has a gym.
In addition, all employees will receive a stipend for home internet.
She teaches two seminars. In addition, she advises eleven graduate students.
The fee covers materials and, in addition, one private lesson a month.
In addition to the salary, the offer includes equity. (preposition — a noun phrase follows, not a clause)
Two of the exhibits, in addition, were never entered into evidence.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of addition (reinforcing)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; moreover, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Moreover, [independent clause]. · [Subject], moreover, [predicate].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides when it sits inside the clause.
entries.meaning: Adds a point that reinforces and outweighs the one before it — the "and what's more" of formal argument. Save it for reasoning: using moreover to add a second item to a grocery list is the classic register mistake.
examples: The device is cheaper than its rivals; moreover, it uses half the power.
Moreover, no one in the department was told the position existed.
The translation is inaccurate. Moreover, whole paragraphs are missing.
The witness had no reason to lie and, moreover, nothing to gain by it.
The lease is expiring; what's more, the rent is going up forty percent.
The statute, moreover, has never once been enforced.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of addition (reinforcing)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; what's more, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. What's more, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], and what's more, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice unless and carries the join — and a comma after it. Front position only; it does not close a clause. Written out as what is more it is a shade more formal and identically punctuated.
entries.meaning: The conversational moreover: it adds a second point and claims the second one hits harder. It belongs to speech, journalism, and sales copy — in a brief or a dissertation, moreover is the expected form.
examples: The tickets were half price; what's more, they came with parking.
He missed the deadline. What's more, he never told anyone he was going to.
The house needs a roof, and what's more, the furnace is thirty years old.
What's more, the same company had been fined twice before.
She finished the course in half the time; what is more, she did it while working nights.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of addition ("besides, moreover"), and in later use of concession ("nevertheless"). Also an archaic postposed preposition meaning "with" (the tools he worked withal).
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; withal, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [verb phrase], withal. · [adjective] and withal [adjective]. · [noun phrase] [relative clause] withal. (archaic preposition — "with")
entries.punctuation: Comma before it in final position and commas on both sides in the middle; a semicolon or period where two independent clauses meet. Mid-phrase it is often printed with no commas at all — a grave and withal kindly man — which is how Shakespeare's editors set it.
entries.meaning: Elizabethan and Victorian English for "besides, and along with that," drifting toward "nevertheless" by the nineteenth century. An American meets it in Shakespeare, the King James Bible, and period novels and essentially nowhere else; written today it reads as costume.
examples: "A goodly gentleman, and withal a scholar." (period diction)
He was a hard master, withal a just one.
The room was cold, dim, and withal strangely comfortable.
She kept the accounts, managed the tenants, and withal found time to write.
The wages were small; withal, the family wanted for nothing.
He had nothing to defend himself withal. (the archaic preposition — "with," not a connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of concession
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; admittedly, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Admittedly, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [be/auxiliary], admittedly, [complement]. · [Subject] [be/auxiliary] admittedly [complement]. (integrated — no commas) · [Independent clause] — admittedly — [continuation].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position; commas or dashes on both sides in mid position. Period or semicolon before it when two independent clauses are involved — never a bare comma.
entries.meaning: Concedes a point against your own argument before you go on to answer it. Granted does the same job conversationally and of course can sound impatient doing it; admittedly is the neutral written form, and it commits the writer to a but somewhere soon after.
examples: Admittedly, the first draft was a mess.
The plan is expensive; admittedly, it is also the only one that has ever worked.
She was, admittedly, the least experienced candidate on the shortlist.
Admittedly, I have never actually read the whole report.
The evidence is thin — admittedly so — but the pattern is hard to ignore.
The design is admittedly dated, but everything still works. (integrated into the clause — no commas)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of concession (two things true at once). Also a plain time adverbial meaning "simultaneously," which belongs to the predicate.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. At the same time, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; at the same time, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [be/auxiliary], at the same time, [complement]. · [Subject] [verb phrase] and, at the same time, [verb phrase]. · [Subject] [verb phrase] at the same time. (literal simultaneity — no commas)
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle. In the literal "simultaneously" sense it is part of the predicate and takes no commas at all: Both alarms went off at the same time.
variants: yet (the coordinating equivalent, which takes a comma)
entries.meaning: Holds two facts in the frame together and asks the reader to keep both: "that is true, and so is this." The connector sense is concessive, not temporal — meanwhile puts two events on a clock, while at the same time puts two judgments on a scale. The literal sense survives right beside it, and only the commas tell them apart.
examples: The layoffs were necessary; at the same time, they were handled badly.
I want her to take the job. At the same time, I'd hate to see her move across the country.
She's the best coach we've had. She is, at the same time, impossible to work for.
The report praises the program and, at the same time, recommends cutting its budget.
Both alarms went off at the same time. (literal simultaneity — no commas, not a connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of contrast (the opposite case)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; contrariwise, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Contrariwise, [independent clause]. · [Subject], contrariwise, [predicate].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle.
entries.meaning: The nineteenth-century ancestor of conversely: it flips the previous statement and asserts the reverse case. In American English it survives mainly in quotation and deliberate whimsy — Tweedledee's "Contrariwise, if it was so, it might be" is where most readers have met it — so conversely is the word for real formal prose.
examples: "Contrariwise," continued Tweedledee, "if it was so, it might be; and if it were so, it would be."
The northern counties gained population; contrariwise, the delta lost a fifth of its residents.
Contrariwise, the older statute imposed no penalty at all.
Heat expands the metal; contrariwise, cold draws it tight.
He believed the letters would clear him. Contrariwise, they were what convicted him.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of contrast (logical reversal)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; conversely, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Conversely, [independent clause]. · [Subject], conversely, [predicate].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides mid-clause.
entries.meaning: Introduces the exact reverse of what was just stated — the same terms with their positions swapped. Use it only when the second clause really is the mirror image; where two ideas are merely being weighed against each other, the honest choice is on the other hand.
examples: Warm weather lifts ice cream sales; conversely, a cold July kills them.
Small firms adapted within months. Conversely, the largest banks took years.
If the price rises, demand falls; conversely, if the price drops, demand climbs.
Adding staff shortened the wait. Conversely, every cut lengthened it.
He finds mornings easy and evenings impossible; his wife, conversely, comes alive after ten.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of concession
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. Even so, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; even so, [independent clause]. · [Subject], even so, [predicate]. · [Independent clause] and, even so, [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle.
entries.meaning: The plain-English nevertheless: it grants everything just said and then holds the original position anyway. However only marks a contrast; even so explicitly concedes first, which is why it so often follows a sentence the speaker has just agreed with.
examples: The tickets were nonrefundable. Even so, the airline gave us a credit.
He apologized twice; even so, she didn't return his calls.
It's a nine-hour drive. Even so, I'd rather go than fly.
We knew the odds going in. Even so, losing hurt.
She had trained for a year and, even so, finished dead last.
The house was, even so, the best thing we saw all weekend.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of concession
entries.pattern: Granted, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Granted. [Independent clause]. · Granted that [clause], [main clause]. (subordinating use)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, and a period or semicolon before it when a full clause precedes — The team is young; granted, so was last year's squad, never a bare comma. It can also stand alone as a one-word sentence (Granted.). Add that and it becomes a subordinating conjunction taking a full clause, punctuated like although: a comma after the granted that clause when that clause comes first, and no comma when it follows the main clause.
entries.meaning: Concedes the other side's point out loud, almost always to set up a but. It is the conversational cousin of admittedly, and it is the one connector in this family that can be a complete turn in a conversation by itself.
examples: Granted, the price is steep — but you'll use it every day.
He's rude. Granted. That doesn't make him wrong.
Granted, I've only seen the first season.
The team is young; granted, so was last year's championship squad.
Granted that the data is five years old, the trend is still unmistakable.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of contrast. Also a subordinating conjunction meaning "no matter how," which does introduce a real adverbial clause.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; however, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. However, [independent clause]. · [Subject], however, [predicate]. · [Independent clause]; [independent clause], however.
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is the textbook comma splice (It rained, however we went is wrong). Comma after it in front position, commas on both sides in the middle, comma before it at the end. The subordinator however takes none of that: However you slice it, the numbers don't work.
entries.meaning: The default contrast connector of written English: it marks its clause as running against the expectation the previous sentence created. But does the same work as a coordinating conjunction with only a comma. Everything that separates the two words follows from however being an adverb — the heavier punctuation, and the freedom to move.
examples: The flight was delayed four hours; however, the airline paid for our hotel.
We expected a crowd. However, only nine people showed up.
The proposal is thorough. The budget, however, is pure fiction.
She promised she'd call. She never did, however.
However you slice it, the numbers don't work. (here however is a subordinator meaning "no matter how," not this connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of contrast (two cases compared). Also in contrast to / in contrast with, a preposition taking a noun phrase.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. In contrast, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; in contrast, [independent clause]. · [Subject], in contrast, [predicate]. · In contrast to [noun phrase], [independent clause]. (preposition)
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it. Adding to or with makes it a preposition that must be followed by a noun phrase: In contrast to last year, sales rose.
variants: in contrast to / in contrast with [noun phrase] (prepositional)
entries.meaning: Sets two things side by side and points at the difference between them. Unlike however, it makes no claim that the second fact is surprising — only that it differs — which makes it the workhorse of comparative analysis and data commentary.
examples: Rural districts lost population. In contrast, the suburbs grew nine percent.
The first novel is spare and cold; in contrast, the second is almost sentimental.
Japanese firms invested in retraining. American firms, in contrast, cut headcount.
In contrast, the control group showed no change at all.
In contrast to her sister, she never touched a piano again. (preposition — a noun phrase follows)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of substitution. Also instead of, a preposition taking a noun phrase or an -ing form.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; instead, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Instead, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; [independent clause] instead. · Instead of [noun phrase / -ing form], [independent clause]. (preposition)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice. Comma after it in front position (often dropped in casual writing); no comma before it in final position, which is where it most often lands in speech: We drove instead.
entries.meaning: Marks its clause as the replacement for something that did not happen — it answers "so what happened instead?" Where rather corrects a statement, instead substitutes an action, and its final-position use (Let's walk instead) has no equivalent among the formal contrast adverbs.
examples: The meeting was canceled; instead, we all went to lunch.
He didn't apologize. Instead, he changed the subject.
We were going to fly. We drove instead.
Instead of driving, we took the train and got there first. (preposition — an -ing form follows, not a clause)
The city rejected the tax increase. Instead, it cut weekend bus service.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of concession
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; nevertheless, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Nevertheless, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [auxiliary] nevertheless [verb phrase]. · [Subject], nevertheless, [predicate]. · [Independent clause]. [Independent clause] nevertheless.
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides mid-clause; in final position the comma before it is usual but often dropped.
entries.meaning: Grants the previous statement in full and then asserts the opposite of what it implied. It and nonetheless are interchangeable in nearly every American context; nevertheless is the older and slightly more frequent of the two, and both are considerably heavier than everyday still or even so.
examples: The evidence was circumstantial; nevertheless, the jury convicted.
She had no formal training. Nevertheless, she rebuilt the engine herself.
The forecast was terrible. We went ahead nevertheless.
The proposal is, nevertheless, the best one we have received.
Two members objected; the motion nevertheless passed eleven to two.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of concession
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; nonetheless, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Nonetheless, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [be/auxiliary] nonetheless [complement]. · [Independent clause]. [Independent clause] nonetheless.
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice. Comma after it in front position, commas on both sides mid-clause. In final position the comma before it is optional: set it off when it is an afterthought (The offer stands, nonetheless), run it in when it belongs to the predicate (The conclusion holds nonetheless).
variants: none the less (older three-word spelling, now rare in American writing)
entries.meaning: Functionally identical to nevertheless — pick either. The only real differences are frequency and rhythm: nonetheless is a syllable shorter, so it falls more comfortably at the end of a sentence, where American writers reach for it slightly more often than for its twin.
examples: The repairs were expensive; nonetheless, the car is worth keeping.
He was outvoted. Nonetheless, he filed a written objection.
The film is uneven, but it is nonetheless the most ambitious thing she has made.
The data are incomplete. The conclusion holds nonetheless.
Nonetheless, the board scheduled a second vote for December.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of concession. Also a preposition, standing either before or after its noun phrase, and with that a formal subordinating conjunction.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; notwithstanding, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Notwithstanding, [independent clause]. · Notwithstanding [noun phrase], [independent clause]. (preposition) · [Noun phrase] notwithstanding, [independent clause]. (preposition, postposed) · Notwithstanding that [clause], [main clause]. (subordinator)
entries.punctuation: As a connector: semicolon or period before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it; but that use is rare. In the far commoner prepositional uses there is no semicolon at all, just the comma that closes the fronted phrase.
entries.meaning: A formal nevertheless, still alive in contracts, statutes, and academic prose. It is much more often a preposition than a connector, and it is the only word in this family that can follow the noun it governs: objections notwithstanding.
examples: The evidence was thin; notwithstanding, the jury convicted.
Notwithstanding, the department went ahead with the hire.
Notwithstanding the storm warnings, the ferry sailed on schedule. (preposition — a noun phrase follows)
The objections of two members notwithstanding, the motion carried. (preposition, placed after its noun)
She had no formal training; notwithstanding, she outperformed every analyst on the desk.
Notwithstanding that the deadline had passed, the clerk accepted the filing. (subordinating conjunction — a full clause follows)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of contradiction
entries.pattern: [Negative statement]. On the contrary, [independent clause]. · [Negative statement]; on the contrary, [independent clause]. · "[Claim]" — "On the contrary, [independent clause]."
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it, comma after it, always — a bare comma between the two clauses is a comma splice. Because it needs something to contradict, it almost never opens a paragraph.
entries.meaning: Denies what was just said and replaces it with the truth. It requires a preceding negative or a claim you are rejecting — and this is the most common misuse in the whole category: on the contrary is not a synonym for on the other hand, which balances two things that can both be true at once.
examples: "You must be exhausted." "On the contrary, I've never felt better."
The reform did not reduce costs; on the contrary, it doubled them.
He isn't shy. On the contrary, he'll talk to anyone who stands still.
On the contrary, the data show the trend running the other way.
Nobody was bored. On the contrary, the whole room was riveted.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of contrast (a balancing consideration)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. On the other hand, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; on the other hand, [independent clause]. · [Subject], on the other hand, [predicate]. · On the one hand, [clause]; on the other hand, [clause].
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it. When it is paired with on the one hand, a semicolon between the two halves is the cleanest choice.
variants: on the one hand … on the other hand (paired)
entries.meaning: Introduces a consideration that pulls the other way without denying the first — both sides stay true, and the reader is asked to weigh them. That is exactly what separates it from on the contrary, which cancels the previous statement outright.
examples: The apartment is small. On the other hand, it's two blocks from the office.
Hiring now is expensive; on the other hand, waiting until spring may cost us the project.
On the one hand, the treatment works; on the other hand, almost nobody can afford it.
He's never managed a team. On the other hand, neither had you at his age.
The used one is half the price. The mileage, on the other hand, would scare me.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of contrast (the entry on the opposite side of the account)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; per contra, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Per contra, [independent clause]. · [Subject], per contra, [predicate].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle. American publishing sets it in roman type rather than italicizing it as a foreign phrase.
entries.meaning: Latin for "on the contrary," literally "by the opposite side" — the phrase comes from double-entry bookkeeping, where the contra entry sits opposite. In American English it is bookish and rare, surviving in accounting (a per contra item), in judicial writing, and in older criticism; conversely or on the other hand is the ordinary choice.
examples: The bank showed a loss for the quarter; per contra, the insurance subsidiary returned nine percent.
Per contra, the defense offered no witness of its own.
The lease is an asset to the tenant and, per contra, a liability to the owner.
Younger readers found the book cold. Per contra, reviewers of his own generation called it his warmest.
The receivable appears in one column and, per contra, in the other as an offsetting charge.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of correction. The same form is also a degree adverb (rather cold), half of the preference idiom would rather, and part of the quasi-coordinator rather than — none of which is this connector.
entries.pattern: [Negative clause]; rather, [independent clause]. · [Negative clause]. Rather, [independent clause]. · [Negative clause] — rather, [independent clause]. · [phrase], or rather, [corrected phrase]. · [Subject] [be] rather [adjective]. (degree adverb) · [Subject] would rather [verb phrase]. (preference idiom)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon, period, or dash before it when two independent clauses are involved — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it. In the or rather correction, commas go on both sides of the whole phrase.
entries.meaning: Corrects the statement just made and puts a more accurate one in its place: "not that — this." Three other rathers have nothing to do with this entry: the degree adverb (rather cold), the preference form (I'd rather stay), and the quasi-coordinator rather than.
examples: It wasn't a negotiation; rather, it was an ultimatum.
The problem isn't the software. Rather, nobody was ever trained to use it.
She didn't refuse — rather, she simply never answered.
We met on Tuesday, or rather, Tuesday night.
The change was not sudden; rather, it took the better part of a decade.
It was rather cold, and I'd rather have stayed home. (degree adverb and preference idiom — neither one is this connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of concession (dismissal). Also regardless of, a preposition taking a noun phrase.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; regardless, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Regardless, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] regardless. · Regardless of [noun phrase], [independent clause]. (preposition)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and no comma before it in final position (He's going regardless). Regardless of takes a noun phrase, and a comma when it is fronted.
entries.meaning: Brushes everything just said aside as not changing the outcome. It is blunter than nevertheless: it does not really concede the point so much as decline to weigh it. Irregardless is nonstandard and widely condemned in American usage — avoid it.
examples: The forecast calls for rain; regardless, the game will be played.
He knows the risks. He's going regardless.
Regardless, somebody has to tell her before Friday.
The budget may be cut. We'll finish the study regardless.
Regardless of the outcome, I'm proud of this team. (preposition — a noun phrase follows)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of concession. The same form is also a plain time adverb meaning "up to now" (She's still asleep) and a degree adverb with comparatives (still colder), neither of which is a connector.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. Still, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; still, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], but still, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [be] still [complement]. (time adverb — no commas)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it; the comma after it in front position is usual but freely dropped in informal writing (Still, I liked it / Still I liked it). Never a bare comma joining the clauses.
entries.meaning: The everyday concessive: "all of that is true, and yet." It is the shortest and least formal member of the nevertheless family. Keep it clear of the time adverb still (She's still asleep), which sits inside the clause and takes no comma at all.
examples: The reviews were brutal. Still, I liked it.
He isn't qualified; still, he'd learn the job in a month.
It's a long shot. Still, somebody has to try.
I know she meant well. Still, she shouldn't have said it in front of everyone.
The car needs a clutch and four tires. Still, it runs.
She's still asleep. (time adverb — inside the clause, no commas, not a connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of concession (pivot)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. That said, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; that said, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it. It does not occur mid-clause or finally; it is a front-position pivot only.
entries.meaning: A conversational pivot: it acknowledges everything just said and then turns against it. Functionally it is nevertheless with a friendlier face, and it is now standard in American business writing and product reviews. It began life as an absolute phrase, which is why the fuller having said that still sounds a shade more careful.
examples: The screen is gorgeous. That said, the battery is a real disappointment.
I trust her judgment; that said, I'd like a second opinion before we sign.
The plan is sound. Having said that, the timeline worries me.
He's the strongest candidate. That being said, he's asking for a lot of money.
That said, nobody is forcing you to decide today.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of contrast (second thought)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. Then again, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; then again, [independent clause]. · But then again, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it. It frequently follows but (But then again, who knows?), which is legal because but is doing the joining and then again is only modifying.
entries.meaning: Introduces a second thought that undercuts the speaker's own previous statement — the connector of visible hesitation. On the other hand weighs two options evenly; then again signals that you are in the act of talking yourself out of what you just said.
examples: I should go to bed. Then again, it's Friday.
She'd never lie about that. Then again, she never mentioned the loan either.
The price seems high. Then again, so is everything downtown.
We could drive; then again, parking down there is impossible.
He's probably fine. But then again, he hasn't called in three days.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of concession. Also a subordinating conjunction, in which use it fronts a dependent clause.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. [Independent clause], though. · [Subject] [verb], though, [continuation]. · Though [clause], [main clause]. (subordinating use — a different animal)
entries.punctuation: As a connector it never opens its clause, so there is no semicolon to place: put a comma before it in final position and commas on both sides mid-clause. The clause it sits in still needs a period or a semicolon in front of it, not a comma. As a subordinator it takes a comma after its own clause when that clause comes first (Though it rained, we went); when the though clause follows, concession is the standard exception to the no-comma rule for trailing subordinate clauses, and the comma stays (We went, though it rained).
entries.meaning: The spoken workhorse of concession, tacked onto the end of a sentence: It's cold. Nice view, though. This use has no formal equivalent — although cannot do it, because although has no adverb life at all. Compare the subordinating though, which fronts a dependent clause and behaves like although in every respect.
examples: The hotel was overpriced. The view was worth it, though.
I don't eat much meat. I'll take a burger, though.
She never wrote back. She did read it, though.
It's a tiny apartment. It's cheap, though.
The repair is expensive. It would, though, solve the problem for good.
Though the rent was high, we took the place. (subordinating conjunction — it fronts a dependent clause)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of parallel weight ("and just as much"). Also a degree adverb inside the clause (equally difficult) and a manner adverb (divided equally), neither of which is a connector.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; equally, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Equally, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [be/auxiliary], equally, [complement]. · [Subject] [be] equally [adjective]. (degree adverb — no commas)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position. Drop the commas and it stops being a connector: Equally, the second study was flawed ("and just as importantly") versus The second study was equally flawed ("flawed to the same degree").
entries.meaning: Presents the next point as carrying exactly the same weight as the last, rather than as merely resembling it — which is what separates it from likewise and similarly, both of which claim likeness of content. British writers front the connector more freely than Americans, who often prefer equally important or just as important.
examples: The schedule is unrealistic; equally, the budget assumes prices that no longer exist.
Teachers need smaller classes. Equally, they need time to plan.
The state has a duty to prosecute; it has, equally, a duty to disclose.
Equally, no one on the board asked where the money had gone.
The second proposal was equally expensive. (degree adverb — "to the same degree," not a connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of comparison (a parallel case)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; likewise, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Likewise, [independent clause]. · [Subject] likewise [verb phrase]. · "Likewise." (as a full reply)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides mid-clause, except when it sits directly before the verb (his lawyer likewise refused), where it takes no commas at all.
entries.meaning: Says that what follows holds in the same way — the matching case, the matching instruction. It also survives as a one-word reply that similarly cannot manage ("Nice working with you." "Likewise."), and in the connector use it is a shade more formal than similarly.
examples: Fold the top edge down; likewise, fold the bottom edge up.
The East Coast offices closed early. Likewise, the Chicago branch sent everyone home.
Freshmen must register by Friday; sophomores, likewise, face a Friday deadline.
He refused to comment, and his lawyer likewise said nothing.
"Great working with you." "Likewise."

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of comparison (a parallel pattern)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; similarly, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Similarly, [independent clause]. · [Subject], similarly, [predicate].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle.
entries.meaning: Introduces a second case that behaves like the first, usually inside an explanation or an argument. Likewise points at sameness of action; similarly points at sameness of pattern, which is why analytical writing prefers it.
examples: Copper conducts heat well; similarly, it conducts electricity.
Toddlers learn words by hearing them repeated. Similarly, adults pick up slang from the people they spend time with.
The northern route floods every spring. The southern route, similarly, closes after heavy rain.
Similarly, the second trial found no difference between the groups.
Freelancers must file quarterly; small partnerships, by the same token, cannot wait until April.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of result (an action taken in response)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; accordingly, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Accordingly, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [verb] accordingly.
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it in front position. In final position (plan accordingly) it is a plain manner adverb and takes no comma at all.
entries.meaning: Says that someone acted in the way the previous fact called for — result plus compliance. Therefore draws a conclusion; accordingly reports an adjustment, so it nearly always has a human agent doing something about it.
examples: Demand had doubled; accordingly, the plant added a second shift.
The regulations changed in January. Accordingly, all permits must be renewed.
The forecast worsened, and the captain accordingly turned back.
Accordingly, the committee has revised its recommendation.
She was told the meeting had moved, and she planned her day accordingly. (manner adverb — "in a way that fits," not a connector)

entries.respell: uz uh rih-ZULT, emphatic az uh rih-ZULT
entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of result. Also as a result of, a preposition taking a noun phrase.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; as a result, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. As a result, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [verb], as a result, [complement]. · As a result of [noun phrase], [independent clause]. (preposition)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it. Add of and it becomes a preposition taking a noun phrase, with a comma after the whole fronted phrase and no semicolon anywhere.
entries.meaning: The plainest way to mark a consequence, and the everyday alternative to consequently in speech and general writing. It states cause and effect without the analytic flavor therefore brings.
examples: The bridge closed for repairs; as a result, the detour added twenty minutes.
Two suppliers went bankrupt. As a result, the line shut down for a week.
She missed the filing deadline and, as a result, lost the appeal.
As a result, ticket prices have nearly doubled since June.
As a result of the storm, half the county lost power. (preposition — a noun phrase follows)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of inference drawn from a category just named. Also a prepositional phrase meaning "in that capacity" or "considered in itself," which sits inside the predicate and takes no commas.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; as such, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. As such, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [be/auxiliary], as such, [complement]. · [Subject] [be] [noun phrase] and as such [verb phrase]. ("in that capacity" — no commas)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle. In the "in that capacity" sense it is part of the predicate and takes no commas at all: She chairs the committee and as such sets the agenda.
variants: in that capacity (the literal sense spelled out)
entries.meaning: Two jobs pull at this phrase, and only one of them is fully settled. Strictly, as such means "in that capacity," and such has to point back to a noun already on the page: He is the trustee, and as such he signs the checks. American writing has also stretched it into a loose therefore with no noun behind it — The vendor missed two deadlines; as such, we canceled the contract — which is now everywhere in business prose and still flagged by careful editors. The rule of thumb: if you cannot say which noun such refers to, write therefore or accordingly instead.
examples: She is the executor of the estate; as such, she is the only person who can sign.
The building is a registered landmark. As such, it cannot be demolished without a hearing.
The document is a draft, and as such it has not been fact-checked. (integrated "in that capacity" sense — no commas)
Interns are students, not staff; they are, as such, paid a stipend rather than a salary.
The vendor missed two deadlines; as such, we canceled the contract. (the loose "therefore" use — common, but therefore is safer in edited prose)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of inference drawn from meaning alone. Also an ordinary prepositional adjunct inside the predicate (settled by definition rather than by evidence).
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; by definition, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. By definition, [independent clause]. · [Subject], by definition, [predicate]. · [Subject] [be] by definition [complement]. (integrated — no commas)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when two independent clauses are joined — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle. Sitting between be and its complement it normally takes no commas: A volunteer is by definition unpaid.
entries.meaning: Says the conclusion follows from what the words mean, not from any evidence — the cheapest and strongest kind of inference, and for that reason a favorite of people arguing in bad faith. Therefore claims the conclusion follows from the facts just given; by definition claims no facts are needed.
examples: The account was opened last week; by definition, it has no payment history.
A volunteer is by definition unpaid.
By definition, an emergency cannot be scheduled.
Every member of the committee is an employee — by definition, none of them is independent.
The policy covers preexisting conditions, which by definition began before the coverage did.

entries.clause: Independent clause or phrase — adverbial link carrying a conclusion over to a neighboring case
entries.pattern: [Independent clause], and by extension, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; by extension, [independent clause]. · [noun phrase] and, by extension, [noun phrase]. · By extension, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Commas on both sides in the middle and a comma after it in front position; a semicolon or period where two independent clauses meet unless and carries the join. It very often attaches to a second noun phrase rather than a clause, and there the pair of commas is all that is needed: the mayor, and by extension the city.
entries.meaning: Carries a conclusion already reached over to something attached to it — typically from a person or a case to the larger body standing behind it. Where by implication draws out what was left unsaid, by extension stretches a stated conclusion to a further target.
examples: The ruling binds the district court and, by extension, every case still pending there.
She controls the foundation; by extension, she controls the museum's entire endowment.
The ad insulted the union and by extension everyone who had ever walked a picket line.
By extension, the same reasoning would void half the contracts in the industry.
The report faults the lab director and, by extension, the university that hired her.

entries.clause: Independent clause or phrase — adverbial link of inference from what was left unsaid
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; by implication, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. By implication, [independent clause]. · [Subject], by implication, [predicate]. · [noun phrase] and, by implication, [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it between two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle.
entries.meaning: Draws out something the previous statement entails without saying — the standard move of legal reasoning and close reading. It is careful where by extension is expansive: the implication is claimed to be in the words already.
examples: The statute names only employers; by implication, contractors fall outside it.
The board approved the budget and, by implication, the layoffs it assumes.
By implication, the letter concedes that the deadline was missed.
She never denied that the meeting took place — by implication, she confirmed it.
The court held that the warranty was disclaimed, by implication, once the buyer inspected the goods.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of result
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; consequently, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Consequently, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [auxiliary] consequently [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle.
entries.meaning: Marks its clause as the outcome the previous clause produced. Where therefore draws a logical conclusion from evidence, consequently reports an actual chain of events — and it is the word most often confused with subsequently, which claims only that the second thing came later.
examples: The vendor missed two deliveries; consequently, we switched suppliers.
Funding was cut in half. Consequently, the survey was reduced to one state.
The pipes froze and, consequently, burst overnight.
Consequently, the department will not be filling the position this year.
He never filed the paperwork; the claim was consequently denied.

entries.register: archaic and dialectal (nonstandard in edited prose)
entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of negative condition ("if not, then")
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; elsewise, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Elsewise, [independent clause]. · [Imperative], elsewise [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position. Dialect writing routinely drops that comma, and the missing comma is part of how the voice is signaled.
entries.meaning: An old variant of otherwise that outlived standard prose in regional American speech and in dialect writing — Appalachia, the Ozarks, cowboy fiction. Reach for it only when you are rendering a voice; in your own prose it reads as an error or an affectation.
examples: Best start early; elsewise you'll be riding home in the dark.
"Pay the man what you owe, elsewise he'll take the horse." (dialect writing)
The stove has to be banked at night. Elsewise, the pipes freeze.
He kept the receipt; elsewise there'd have been no proving it.
"Elsewise," she said, "we'd have lost the whole crop."

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of inference. Also used before a bare noun phrase with no verb, and separately as a time adverb meaning "from now" (two weeks hence).
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; hence [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Hence, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; hence [noun phrase]. · [Independent clause] — hence [noun phrase]. · [Independent clause], and hence [independent clause]. · [Time expression] hence. (time adverb — "from now")
entries.punctuation: Semicolon, period, or dash before it — a bare comma joining the two clauses is a comma splice, and the only way to get a comma there is to add a coordinator (The vote was tied, and hence the measure failed). The comma after it is optional and is normally omitted before a bare noun phrase — hence the delay, never hence, the delay.
entries.meaning: A compressed therefore, and the only member of this family that regularly appears with no verb after it at all: Snow was forecast — hence the empty parking lot. In full clauses it is terser and more literary than therefore. The time adverb hence (two weeks hence, "from now") is a separate word class, not a variant of this connector.
examples: The bridge was out; hence the four-hour detour.
The samples were contaminated. Hence, the results were discarded.
He grew up in Naples, hence the accent.
Two servers failed at once; hence the outage.
The vote was tied, and hence the measure failed.
The report is due two weeks hence. (time adverb — "from now," a different word class)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of result. Also in consequence of, a preposition taking a noun phrase.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; in consequence, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. In consequence, [independent clause]. · [Subject], in consequence, [predicate]. · In consequence of [noun phrase], [independent clause]. (preposition)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle. The prepositional in consequence of takes no semicolon, only the comma that closes a fronted phrase.
entries.meaning: The heavier, older sibling of consequently, at home in official reports, judgments, and nineteenth-century prose. American editors generally prefer consequently or as a result; in consequence survives where the writing is deliberately formal.
examples: The line was cut on Tuesday; in consequence, three shifts lost their pay.
The company misstated its reserves. In consequence, the auditors resigned.
She had, in consequence, no way of knowing that the account was overdrawn.
In consequence of the flooding, the courthouse was closed for a week. (preposition — a noun phrase follows, not a clause)
Two directors voted against the merger and, in consequence, were not renominated.

entries.clause: Independent clause or phrase — adverbial link of practical equivalence ("what it amounts to"). Distinct from the predicative phrase in effect meaning "in force" (the rule is still in effect), which is not a connector.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; in effect, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. In effect, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [verb], in effect, [complement]. · [Subject] [be] in effect. ("in force" — not a connector)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle. The "in force" sense sits bare at the end of the predicate with no commas at all.
entries.meaning: Restates what was just said as what it actually amounts to once the formalities are stripped away — usually something blunter than the official version. In essence reduces a thing to its core; in effect reports the practical upshot, and it is the standard way to say that something is one thing on paper and another in practice.
examples: The company stopped answering our letters; in effect, the contract was over.
The fee applies to every transaction. In effect, it is a tax on paying your rent.
She was given no work and no office — in effect, she had been fired.
The amendment, in effect, repeals the section it claims to clarify.
The ordinance is still in effect. ("in force" — the predicative phrase, not a connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of result one link further along a chain. Also a plain adverbial meaning "one after another" (the judges spoke in turn), which belongs to the predicate and takes no commas.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; in turn, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. In turn, [independent clause]. · [Subject], in turn, [predicate]. · [Independent clause], which in turn [verb phrase]. · [Subject] [verb phrase] in turn. (literal "one after another" — no commas)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle. Inside a relative clause (which in turn raised prices) it is integrated and takes no commas of its own. In the literal "one after another" sense it sits in the predicate, uncommaed: Each witness testified in turn.
variants: which in turn (inside a relative clause)
in its turn (formal and less common)
entries.meaning: Marks the next link in a chain of consequences: A causes B, and B in turn causes C. That is exactly what separates it from as a result, which reports one effect and stops; in turn promises that the effect has itself become a cause. It is the connector of economic, mechanical, and epidemiological explanation, and the clause it opens is usually where the paragraph was headed all along.
examples: The tariff raised the cost of steel; in turn, appliance prices climbed.
Fewer flights meant fewer hotel bookings. In turn, the whole downtown lost its winter business.
Higher rates cool construction, which in turn softens demand for lumber.
Cutting the night bus stranded the hospital's overnight staff; the hospital, in turn, started paying for cabs.
Each of the six speakers was given four minutes and answered questions in turn. (literal "one after another" — no commas, not a connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause or phrase — adverbial link of inference ("by that fact alone")
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; ipso facto, [independent clause]. · Ipso facto, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [be] ipso facto [complement]. (integrated — no commas) · [Subject] [verb], ipso facto, [complement].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it between two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position. Inside a predicate it takes no commas: the sale is ipso facto void. American legal style sets it in roman, not italics.
entries.meaning: Latin for "by the fact itself": the consequence follows from the bare fact, with no further finding required. It lives in contracts, canon law, and judicial opinions — an ipso facto clause ends an agreement the moment a party files for bankruptcy — and in ordinary argument it usually signals someone reaching for authority they have not earned.
examples: A member who fails to pay dues for two years ipso facto forfeits membership.
The filing of a petition renders the lease, ipso facto, terminable at the lessor's option.
Excommunication in such cases is incurred ipso facto, without any declaration by the ordinary.
He assumed that because the study was published, it was ipso facto reliable.
The property was pledged as security; ipso facto, the bank's claim outranks the others.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of negative condition ("if not"). Also a manner adverb meaning "differently" (I couldn't have done otherwise) and a modifier meaning "in other respects" (an otherwise quiet street).
entries.pattern: [Imperative or statement]; otherwise, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Otherwise, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; otherwise [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], but otherwise [independent clause]. ("in all other respects") · [Subject] [auxiliary] otherwise [verb phrase]. (manner adverb — "differently")
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it, comma after it in front position — though the comma is often dropped in short warnings (Hurry; otherwise we'll be late). Never a bare comma between the clauses.
variants: or else (the coordinating equivalent, which does take a comma)
entries.meaning: States what will follow if the previous statement is not acted on: "if that doesn't happen, this will." It carries a second, unrelated connector sense — "in all other respects" (The soup was cold; otherwise the meal was excellent) — and a manner sense (I couldn't have done otherwise).
examples: Leave by six; otherwise, you'll hit traffic on the bridge.
Write it down. Otherwise, you'll forget by Thursday.
The deposit is due Friday; otherwise the room goes back on the market.
She has a cough. Otherwise, she's fine. (the "in all other respects" sense)
We got lost twice, but otherwise the trip was perfect.
She could hardly have done otherwise. (manner adverb — "differently," not a connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of logical conclusion
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; therefore, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Therefore, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [auxiliary] therefore [verb phrase]. · [Subject] [verb] and is, therefore, [complement].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when two independent clauses are joined; comma after it in front position, commas on both sides in the middle. It rained, therefore we stayed in is a comma splice — the single most-tested error in this category.
entries.meaning: Draws a conclusion that follows logically from what came before — the connector of proofs, contracts, and arguments. So does the same work in speech as a coordinating conjunction with just a comma. The whole difference is grammatical class, and the punctuation follows from it.
examples: The witness was out of the country; therefore, she could not have made the call.
Every flight was full. Therefore, we rented a car and drove.
The two triangles have equal sides and therefore equal angles.
The clause is unenforceable and is, therefore, void.
It rained all afternoon; therefore, the game was postponed to Sunday.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of result. Also a manner adverb meaning "in this way," and a linker to -ing participles.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; thus [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Thus, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [verb phrase] and thus [verb phrase]. · [Independent clause], thus [-ing participle phrase]. · Thus [verb] [subject]. (literary inversion) · [Verb] [object] thus. (manner adverb — "in this way")
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and the comma after it is optional and usually dropped (thus the findings cannot be generalized). No semicolon is needed when it introduces a participle, since no second clause exists: …washed out, thus cutting the town off.
entries.meaning: Carries both "therefore" and "in this way," and the second sense is what separates it from therefore: Hold the brush thus means "like this." As a connector it is the most literary of the result adverbs, and it is the only one that comfortably heads a participial phrase.
examples: The sample was too small; thus the findings cannot be generalized.
The road washed out, thus cutting the town off for two days.
Thus began the longest winter in the region's history.
Each part is machined separately and thus can be replaced on its own.
The treaty was never ratified. Thus, the old rules still apply.
Hold the brush thus, at a shallow angle to the paper. (manner adverb — "in this way")

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of purpose: the means adopted to reach a goal the previous sentence stated
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. To that end, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; to that end, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [verb phrase] to that end. · To this end, [independent clause]. (same connector, pointing at a goal just stated)
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it, comma after it in front position; no comma before it in final position (the company hired two lobbyists to that end). A bare comma between the clauses is a comma splice, exactly as with every other adverb in this file.
entries.meaning: Names the action taken in service of a goal already stated — the forward-looking mirror of as a result, which reports what a cause produced. It belongs to proposals, mission statements, and grant applications, and it needs a stated goal in front of it or it has nothing to point at.
examples: The district wants every third grader reading at grade level. To that end, it has added an hour of literacy instruction a day.
We need the report by Friday; to that end, I've cleared your afternoon.
The foundation exists to protect the watershed. To this end, it has bought four thousand acres of riverfront.
The board resolved to cut emissions in half by 2030 and hired a consultant to that end.
To that end, the university will match the first million dollars raised.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of sequence
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; afterward, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Afterward, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] afterward.
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it in front position; no comma before it in final position (We got coffee afterward).
variants: afterwards (the standard British form, and common in American speech; afterward without the -s is the preferred form in American edited prose)
entries.meaning: Places its clause later in time than the last one. Unlike then, it does not claim immediate succession — an afterward can be hours or years later — and unlike subsequently it is comfortable in conversation.
examples: The ceremony ran long; afterward, everyone crowded into the lobby.
We toured the plant. Afterward, the manager answered questions for an hour.
She apologized to him privately afterward.
Afterward, nobody could agree on what had actually been said.
He was fine during the interview and fell apart afterwards. (the -s form — British in print, ordinary in American speech)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of sequence (final item). Also a plain time adverb meaning "at long last," which sits inside the clause and takes no commas.
entries.pattern: Finally, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Finally, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; finally, [independent clause]. · [Subject] finally [verb]. (time adverb, not a connector)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when a full clause precedes — never a bare comma — and a comma after it in front position when it closes a list. When it means "at long last" it sits inside the clause and takes no commas at all; that position difference is the only signal of which sense you have.
entries.meaning: Marks the last item in a sequence of steps or arguments. Keep it apart from the time adverb meaning "at long last" (The bus finally came), which reports relief rather than structure.
examples: Finally, add the zest and stir once.
We considered cost, then schedule; finally, we looked at risk.
Finally, I'd like to thank the volunteers who stayed until midnight.
The bus finally came. (time adverb — no comma, no connector reading)
Finally, no proposal may exceed twelve pages.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of enumeration that also ranks: the first item and the most important one at once
entries.pattern: First and foremost, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; first and foremost, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [be], first and foremost, [complement]. · [Subject] [be] first and foremost [complement]. (integrated — no commas)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, with a period or semicolon before it when a clause precedes — a bare comma there is a comma splice. Inside a predicate it is integrated and takes no commas: she is first and foremost a trial lawyer.
entries.meaning: Opens a list and marks its first item as the one that matters most — a double duty that plain first does not do. Speeches and mission statements have worn it smooth, so in tight prose above all or a bare first often reads better.
examples: First and foremost, no one was hurt.
First and foremost, the district needs teachers; the buildings can wait.
She is, first and foremost, a trial lawyer.
The job is first and foremost about showing up on time. (integrated — no commas)
First and foremost, I want to thank the people who stayed late all week.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of enumeration opening a list, most often a list of objections
entries.pattern: First off, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. First off, [independent clause]. · For starters, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position and a period or semicolon before it — never a bare comma joining the two clauses. Front position only: neither form sits inside a clause or at the end of one.
entries.meaning: The spoken opener of a list, and in American English it very often introduces the first item in a list of complaints: First off, nobody asked me. For starters is the same move with more edge — it implies the list could go on a while — and neither belongs in formal writing, where first does the work.
examples: First off, that is not what the email said.
First off, we can't afford it; second, we don't have the space.
For starters, the permit was never filed.
"What's wrong with the plan?" "First off, it's illegal."
For starters, he showed up two hours late and without the paperwork.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of enumeration. The same words are ordinary ordinal adjectives and nouns elsewhere (the first draft, she finished second); only the fronted, comma-marked use is a connector.
entries.pattern: First, [independent clause]. Second, [independent clause]. Third, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; second, [independent clause]. · [Statement]: first, [item]; second, [item]. · First [noun phrase] [verb phrase]. (ordinal adjective — no comma)
entries.punctuation: Comma after each one in front position. Each ordinal introduces its own sentence, so a period or semicolon separates the items — the series never runs on commas alone, which would be a string of comma splices.
variants: firstly, secondly, thirdly (equally correct, a shade more formal; American style guides generally prefer the short forms)
entries.meaning: Numbers the steps of an argument or a set of instructions and tells the reader how many more are coming. The one rule that matters is consistency: do not mix the two series (first … secondly), and do not start with firstly unless you are prepared to finish with fourthly.
examples: First, preheat the oven. Second, grease the pan.
There are two problems: first, the cost; second, the timeline.
First, the deadline has passed. Second, the form was never signed. Third, nobody told the client.
Firstly, I'd question the sample size.
First of all, that is not what I said.
The first draft ran three times too long. (ordinal adjective — no comma, not a connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of time (from now on)
entries.pattern: Henceforth, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; henceforth, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [auxiliary] henceforth [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides mid-clause.
variants: from now on / going forward (the everyday equivalents)
entries.meaning: Announces that a new rule holds for all future time. It is genuinely formal — statutes, bylaws, and proclamations — and in ordinary American speech from now on is what people actually say.
examples: Henceforth, all requests must be submitted through the portal.
The building will henceforth be known as the Hartley Center.
The treaty was signed in May; henceforth, the border was closed to trade.
Henceforth, no member may vote by proxy.
She resigned from the board and henceforth refused to discuss the company at all.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of time (up to now)
entries.pattern: Hitherto, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [auxiliary] hitherto [verb phrase]. · [noun phrase] hitherto [past participle].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position; no commas when it sits before the verb or modifies a participle (hitherto unknown). Semicolon or period before it if a second independent clause precedes — a bare comma there is a comma splice.
entries.meaning: "Up to this point" — it names the state of affairs that held before the change you are about to describe. It is the past-facing mirror of henceforth, and it sounds distinctly bookish in American speech.
examples: Hitherto, the treaty had been observed by both sides.
The technique revealed structures hitherto invisible to microscopy.
Sales had hitherto been confined to the Northeast; the new stores changed that.
The archive had been sealed for eighty years; hitherto, not one of these letters had been published.
She published data that had hitherto been held privately by the manufacturer.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of sequence meaning "at the first stage, before anything else is tried." Distinct from the fixed legal phrase court of first instance, which names the court where a case is first heard.
