entries.pattern: In the first instance, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; in the first instance, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [modal] [verb phrase], in the first instance, [continuation]. · [Subject] should [verb phrase] in the first instance.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, commas on both sides in the middle, and a comma before it at the end; a period or semicolon where two independent clauses meet.
entries.meaning: Names the first step of a procedure, with the strong implication that further steps exist if it fails — which is why it belongs to policies, statutes, and grievance procedures rather than to narrative. It is commoner in British than American usage, and an American reader hears it as institutional language.
examples: In the first instance, complaints should be raised with the immediate supervisor.
Applications are reviewed, in the first instance, by the department chair.
The matter is heard by a magistrate in the first instance, with an appeal to the circuit court.
In the first instance, the agency asked only for the missing schedules.
Funding is allocated in the first instance to districts with the highest poverty rates.

entries.clause: Independent clause — two jobs. Fronted, it enumerates the first of several reasons; at the end of a clause it points back to the beginning of the whole business and means "before any of this ever started."
entries.pattern: In the first place, [independent clause]. · In the first place, [independent clause]; in the second place, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] in the first place. (retrospective — no comma before it)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, with a period or semicolon before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice. In the retrospective sense it closes the clause and takes no comma at all: Why did you sign it in the first place?
variants: in the second place (the matching enumerator)
entries.meaning: Fronted, it opens an argument with the first of a numbered set of reasons and promises more. Stranded at the end, it makes a different point entirely — that the thing should never have been started — and it carries an audible note of complaint.
examples: In the first place, the deadline had already passed.
In the first place, she never agreed to it; in the second place, she wasn't even in the country.
Why did you lend him the car in the first place? (retrospective — no comma)
In the first place, the road isn't ours to close.
The permit should never have been issued in the first place.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of enumeration (final item)
entries.pattern: Lastly, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Lastly, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; lastly, [independent clause]. · [item], [item], and, lastly, [final item]. (inside a list)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when a full clause precedes — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it. It fronts its own clause; the one other place it appears is inside a list, where it takes commas on both sides.
entries.meaning: Closes an enumerated list. It is slightly more formal than finally and has one practical advantage over it: lastly has no "at long last" sense, so it can never be misread as a time adverb.
examples: Lastly, please initial the bottom of each page.
We looked at price, then at reliability; lastly, we considered resale value.
Lastly, I want to say something about the budget.
The kit contains a wrench, two gaskets, and, lastly, a tube of sealant.
Lastly, no refunds will be issued after the thirtieth.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of simultaneity
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; meanwhile, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Meanwhile, [independent clause]. · [Subject], meanwhile, [predicate].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle.
variants: in the meantime (preferred for the waiting period between two events)
entries.meaning: Points at what was happening elsewhere at the same time. In journalism it often carries a dry contrast — The mayor promised action; meanwhile, the potholes got worse — where the simultaneity is the joke. Use in the meantime when you mean the interval between two events rather than a parallel scene.
examples: I'll start the grill; meanwhile, you can chop the onions.
The trial dragged into its third week. Meanwhile, the company kept selling the product.
Her flight was canceled. In the meantime, the hotel gave away her room.
The council debated the wording for an hour; the building, meanwhile, went on flooding.
Meanwhile, back at the office, nobody had noticed she was gone.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of sequence. Also a determiner-like adjective (next week, the next chapter) and part of the preposition next to.
entries.pattern: Next, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Next, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [verb] next. · Next [noun phrase] [verb phrase]. (adjective — no comma) · [clause] next to [noun phrase]. (part of a preposition — not this connector)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position; each step is normally its own sentence, so a period does the separating, and a semicolon is required if you run two clauses together — a bare comma there is a comma splice. In final position (What happens next?) it takes no comma.
entries.meaning: The step-by-step connector of recipes, instructions, and narration. It differs from then only in explicitness: next announces that this is the following item in a list you have already promised.
examples: Next, whisk the eggs into the warm milk.
We interviewed the staff. Next, we pulled three years of invoices.
Next, the officer asked for my registration.
Attach the two brackets. Next, tighten the bolts a quarter turn each.
Nobody knew what would happen next.
We're moving next month, into the house next to the school. (adjective and preposition — neither one is this connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of time (earlier point). Also a plain time adverb inside the predicate and a modifier of a participle or adjective (previously undisclosed), neither of which takes commas.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; previously, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Previously, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [auxiliary] previously [verb phrase]. · Previously [past participle] [noun phrase] [verb phrase]. (modifier — no commas)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it in front position; no commas when it stands directly before the main verb (had previously testified).
variants: formerly (of a former state, name, or title)
entries.meaning: Points back to a time earlier than the one under discussion. It is the reporting word: previously belongs to résumés, court records, and news copy, where earlier or before that would be the conversational choice.
examples: The building is now a library; previously, it housed the county jail.
Previously, she had worked as a translator in Geneva.
Two witnesses had previously given the same account to police.
The rate was fixed at four percent. Previously, it floated with the market.
Previously undisclosed emails surfaced during discovery. (modifying a participle — no commas, not a connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of sequence
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; subsequently, [independent clause]. · Subsequently, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [auxiliary] subsequently [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it in front position; no commas before the main verb (was subsequently withdrawn).
entries.meaning: "Afterward," in the register of a report or a court record. It means only that the second event came later — it makes no causal claim at all, which is precisely where it parts company with consequently, the word it is most often confused with.
examples: The charges were subsequently dropped.
He resigned in March; subsequently, two of his deputies left as well.
Subsequently, the manufacturer recalled every unit sold that year.
The paper was published in 2019 and was subsequently retracted.
She was hired as an intern and subsequently promoted twice in one year.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of sequence, or of inference drawn from a condition. Also a plain time adverb meaning "at that time" (we lived in Ohio then) and, before a title, an attributive adjective (the then governor).
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; then [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], and then [independent clause]. · If [clause], then [main clause]. · [Independent clause] then. (inference, informal) · the then [noun]. (attributive adjective — no commas)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it joins two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice unless a coordinator carries the join (and then) — and normally no comma after it (Then we drove home, not Then, we drove home). In the if … then pattern the comma belongs after the if clause, not after then.
variants: in that case (for the inference sense only)
entries.meaning: Two connector jobs. First, next in a sequence: Brown the onions; then add the garlic. Second, the conclusion drawn from a condition: If that's true, then we have a problem. The second job pairs it with if so tightly that it feels like a conjunction, but it still passes the movement test — If that's true, we have a problem, then — which a real conjunction never would.
examples: Preheat the oven; then mix the dry ingredients.
We finished the paperwork, and then the power went out.
If the flight is canceled, then we'll drive.
"She already left." "Then there's no point waiting."
First he denied it; then he blamed the intern.
We lived in Ohio then, and the then governor was a family friend. (plain time adverb and attributive adjective — neither one is this connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of sequence ("after that point")
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; thereafter, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Thereafter, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [verb phrase] thereafter. · [Time expression] thereafter, [independent clause]. (as in shortly thereafter)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position. In final position it belongs to the predicate and takes no comma before it: The rate resets annually thereafter. In the fixed phrases shortly thereafter and soon thereafter, the comma follows the whole phrase, not the adverb.
variants: shortly thereafter / soon thereafter (the usual fixed phrases)
entries.meaning: "After that point," anchored to a moment the text has already fixed. It is afterward in the register of a lease, a statute, or a chronicle, and it differs from henceforth in where it stands: henceforth counts forward from the moment of writing, thereafter from a reference point inside the story. It needs that reference point — with nothing before it for there to name, it reads as a drafting error.
examples: The lease runs for three years; thereafter, it renews month to month.
She served two terms on the council. Thereafter, she never held public office again.
Interest is fixed for the first sixty months and floats thereafter.
The dam failed at 4:10 a.m.; shortly thereafter, the sirens sounded downstream.
Thereafter, every shipment was inspected at the border.

entries.clause: Independent clause or phrase — an adverbial back-reference identifying something already stated in the same document
entries.pattern: [Independent clause], as aforesaid, [continuation]. · [noun phrase] as aforesaid. · As aforesaid, [independent clause]. · the said [noun] as aforesaid.
entries.punctuation: Commas on both sides when it interrupts a clause; no commas when it trails the noun phrase it points back to (the premises as aforesaid). Between two independent clauses a semicolon or period is still required, as with any conjunctive adverb.
entries.meaning: The drafter's back-pointer: "the thing I already identified above," so that the instrument need not describe it twice. It belongs to deeds, leases, wills, and pleadings — outside a legal document it reads as parody, and plain-language drafting guides push writers toward as stated above or simple repetition of the name.
examples: The Seller, as aforesaid, shall deliver clear title on or before the closing date.
The rent as aforesaid shall be payable in twelve equal monthly installments.
As aforesaid, the parties have agreed to submit any dispute to arbitration in Cook County.
Witness my hand and seal the day and year as aforesaid.
The said premises as aforesaid are conveyed subject to all easements of record.

entries.respell: az it WUR, reduced uz it WUR
entries.clause: No clause of its own — a parenthetical comment on the wording just used, marking it as figurative or approximate. The verb is a fossilized subjunctive (were), which is why it never changes tense.
entries.pattern: [clause], as it were, [continuation]. · [phrase] — as it were — [continuation]. · [Independent clause], as it were.
entries.punctuation: Always fenced by commas or dashes, wherever it sits, including the comma before it when it closes a sentence. It joins no clauses, so it never takes a semicolon of its own.
entries.meaning: Apologizes for a metaphor by marking the words just used as not literally true. So to speak does the same job in plainer clothes; as it were carries an unmistakably donnish tone, and used more than once a page it reads as fussy.
examples: He became, as it were, the family's accountant, though nobody ever paid him.
The committee had painted itself into a corner, as it were.
She was the ghost in the machine, as it were — everywhere and nowhere in the company's records.
We were, as it were, guests in our own house that summer.
The novel is a map of the city, as it were, drawn entirely from memory.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (phrasal — a noun phrase used as a connector)
entries.clause: No clause of its own in the connector use — it labels what follows as the illustration of the claim just made. It is also an ordinary noun phrase inside a clause (a case in point is the 2019 audit).
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. Case in point: [example]. · [Independent clause] — case in point, [example]. · A case in point is [noun phrase]. (ordinary noun phrase) · [Noun phrase] is a case in point.
entries.punctuation: A period or dash before it, and a colon or comma after it — the colon is the usual American choice, because what follows is normally a fragment rather than a clause. As a full noun phrase inside a sentence it takes no punctuation at all.
entries.meaning: Presents the next thing said as the proof of the point just made, and it is the one member of the exemplification family that is comfortable as a bare fragment. For example offers one of many and claims nothing about it; case in point claims the example is decisive.
examples: Deferred maintenance always costs more later. Case in point: the roof of the middle school.
Small towns lose their pharmacies first. Case in point — Rushville, which has had none since 2021.
The agency approves nearly everything it reviews; the pipeline permit is a case in point.
Case in point: last winter's outage, which lasted six days.
A case in point is the 1994 amendment, which nobody has ever invoked.

entries.clause: No clause of its own — it introduces one or more sample items inside a clause
entries.pattern: [clause] (e.g., [item], [item]). · [noun phrase] — e.g., [item] — [continuation]. · [clause], e.g., [item].
entries.punctuation: American style keeps both periods and puts a comma after the abbreviation — e.g., — every time. It normally lives inside parentheses, dashes, or commas, and it is never followed by etc. in the same list, since e.g. already announces that the list is partial. If it ends a sentence, its final period does double duty; do not type a second one.
variants: eg / e.g (British and web styles; American editing keeps both periods)
entries.meaning: From Latin exempli gratia, "for the sake of an example." It introduces a sample, never a complete list — and that is the entire difference between it and i.e., which restates exactly what was meant. Spell it out as for example in running text; keep the abbreviation for parentheses and notes.
examples: Bring something warm (e.g., a fleece or a heavy sweater).
Citrus fruits — e.g., lemons, limes, and grapefruit — grow well in the valley.
Avoid oily fish, e.g., mackerel and sardines, for two days before the test.
Some states (e.g., Nevada) have no state income tax.
The policy covers minor repairs, e.g., a cracked windshield.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of exemplification
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; for example, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. For example, [independent clause]. · [Subject], for example, [predicate]. · [noun phrase], for example.
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when two independent clauses are joined — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position, commas on both sides in the middle, and a comma before it at the end.
variants: for instance (interchangeable in every American context)
say (informal: take a small town, say, Burlington)
entries.meaning: Introduces one illustration of a general point. It says nothing about the size of the whole set — for a complete list you want namely, and for a restatement of the same idea, that is.
examples: Some birds don't migrate. Cardinals, for example, stay all winter.
The rules are inconsistent; for example, you can appeal a fine but not a suspension.
For instance, last April that same server went down twice in a week.
Many household costs have risen — insurance, for example, is up nine percent.
Take a small city like Burlington, for example.

entries.clause: Independent clause or phrase — adverbial link of exemplification
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; for instance, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. For instance, [independent clause]. · [Subject], for instance, [predicate]. · [noun phrase], for instance.
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it between two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position, commas on both sides in the middle, and a comma before it when it trails a noun phrase.
entries.meaning: Interchangeable with for example in every American context; the only real difference is rhythm, and for instance is slightly the commoner of the two in speech and in mid-sentence position. Like for example, it offers one illustration and claims nothing about the rest of the set.
examples: Some fees are unavoidable; the recording fee, for instance, is set by the county.
For instance, the Cleveland office closed three weeks before anyone was told.
Take the school calendar, for instance — it hasn't changed since 1978.
Older houses hide their problems. For instance, the wiring in this one is cloth-wrapped.
She has a talent for the small kindness — remembering birthdays, for instance.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of clarification, announcing that what follows resolves an ambiguity rather than adding a new obligation
entries.pattern: For the avoidance of doubt, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. For the avoidance of doubt, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; for the avoidance of doubt, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it, and a period or semicolon before it — a bare comma joining the two clauses is a comma splice. Front position: drafters put it at the head of its own sentence or its own numbered subsection.
variants: provided, however, that (which changes the deal rather than clarifying it)
entries.meaning: A drafter's flag meaning "this sentence only spells out what the agreement already says." Litigators treat it warily — a clause that truly adds nothing is unnecessary, and one that adds something has been mislabeled — but it is standard furniture in commercial contracts and, increasingly, in corporate email.
examples: For the avoidance of doubt, nothing in this Section limits the Company's rights under Section 4.2.
For the avoidance of doubt, the Fee is exclusive of all applicable taxes.
The license is non-transferable. For the avoidance of doubt, a change of control constitutes a transfer.
For the avoidance of doubt, no partnership or joint venture is created by this Agreement.
For the avoidance of doubt, the parties agree that time is of the essence with respect to each delivery date.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (phrasal — a fixed discourse marker)
entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of self-correction and restatement. It is frozen in the first-person present: I meant is a report of what somebody said, not this connector.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause] — I mean, [corrected clause]. · [Independent clause]. I mean, [independent clause]. · [phrase], I mean, [corrected phrase].
entries.punctuation: A dash or period before it and a comma after it, with commas on both sides when it interrupts. A bare comma joining two independent clauses across it is still a comma splice in edited prose, though transcripts and dialogue print it that way to keep the rhythm of speech.
entries.meaning: The spoken counterpart of that is: it repairs, sharpens, or defends what was just said. In fast conversation it has also become a plain turn-opener with no repair work left in it (I mean, who wouldn't?), which is why it grates on the page — use that is or in other words there.
examples: It's expensive — I mean, not outrageous, but more than I wanted to spend.
She's my cousin. I mean, technically my second cousin.
We left around nine, I mean, closer to nine thirty.
I mean, what was he supposed to do, walk home?
He was upset. I mean, he was really upset.

entries.clause: No clause of its own — it introduces a restatement inside a clause
entries.pattern: [clause] (i.e., [restatement]). · [noun phrase] — i.e., [restatement] — [continuation]. · [clause], i.e., [restatement].
entries.punctuation: Both periods stay, and American style puts a comma after the abbreviation — i.e., — every time. Like e.g., it belongs inside parentheses, dashes, or commas rather than at the head of a sentence.
variants: ie / i.e (British and web styles; American editing keeps both periods)
entries.meaning: From Latin id est, "that is." It renames or restates the preceding phrase exactly; it never introduces a mere example. The test is substitution: if "in other words" fits, i.e. is right, and if "for example" fits, you wanted e.g.
examples: The fee is due at the end of the quarter (i.e., March 31).
Only full members — i.e., those who have paid dues for two years — may vote.
The device runs on a single cell, i.e., one AA battery.
Payment is due on receipt, i.e., the day the invoice arrives.
She works in the humanities, i.e., the departments hit hardest by the cuts.

entries.clause: Independent clause or phrase — adverbial link of restatement that reduces something to its core
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; in essence, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. In essence, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [be], in essence, [complement]. · [Subject] [be] in essence [complement]. (integrated — no commas)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle.
entries.meaning: Strips a complicated statement down to what it fundamentally is. In effect reports the practical result; in essence reports the underlying nature — and the two are not interchangeable, though speakers swap them constantly.
examples: The proposal runs ninety pages; in essence, it asks the city for a tax abatement.
In essence, both sides agree about the facts and disagree about what they mean.
The dispute is, in essence, about who owns the parking lot.
The new rule is in essence the old rule with a longer form to fill out.
In essence, the drug slows the disease without stopping it.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of restatement
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. In other words, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; in other words, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] — in other words, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Period, semicolon, or dash before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it. It is a front-position connector; it does not sit at the end of a clause.
entries.meaning: Restates what was just said in plainer terms, or spells out what it really amounts to. Where that is narrows and specifies, in other words translates — and in conversation it very often introduces a blunt paraphrase the other person may not enjoy hearing.
examples: The account is overdrawn; in other words, we are out of money.
The position was eliminated. In other words, he was fired.
She said she'd "circle back in Q3" — in other words, never.
In other words, nobody read the contract before signing it.
The results were not statistically significant; in other words, the drug did nothing.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of specification (singling one case out of a set already mentioned). Also a postmodifier attached directly to a noun phrase.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; in particular, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. In particular, [independent clause]. · [Subject], in particular, [predicate]. · [Noun phrase] in particular [verb phrase]. (postmodifier — no commas)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle. Attached to a noun phrase it takes no commas at all: one paragraph in particular worried the lawyers.
entries.meaning: Picks one member out of a group already named and says it matters most. For example offers a sample and claims nothing about it; in particular claims prominence — this one above the others — which is why it so often carries the weight of the argument.
examples: The storm damaged three schools; in particular, the roof of the high school gym came down.
Costs are up across the board. In particular, insurance has nearly doubled since 2019.
One paragraph in particular worried the lawyers. (attached to the noun phrase — no commas)
Older drivers, in particular, benefit from the larger displays.
In particular, no employee may accept a gift worth more than fifty dollars.

entries.clause: No clause of its own — it introduces the exact identification of something already named in general terms
entries.pattern: [clause], namely, [list]. · [clause] — namely, [item]. · [noun phrase]: namely, [item].
entries.punctuation: A comma, dash, or colon before it; the comma after it is optional (namely, the cost and namely the cost are both standard). It does not take a semicolon, because what follows is a phrase, not a clause.
entries.meaning: Introduces the complete and exact identification of what was just referred to generally — all of it, not a sample. For example offers one of many; namely closes the set, which is why it is the safer word in contracts and specifications.
examples: Only one thing worried her, namely the cost.
Three states border the lake, namely Ohio, Michigan, and Indiana.
The committee has a single job: namely, to decide whether the site is safe.
He left out the most important detail — namely, that he had already resigned.
Two witnesses were called, viz., the driver and the paramedic.

entries.clause: Independent clause or phrase — adverbial link of specification. Also a plain manner adverb meaning "expressly, for that purpose," which sits in the predicate.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; specifically, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Specifically, [independent clause]. · [clause], specifically, [noun phrase]. · [Subject] [be/auxiliary] specifically [verb phrase]. (manner adverb — no commas)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle. Before a bare phrase rather than a clause, a comma or dash is enough. As a manner adverb inside the predicate it takes no commas: the grant was specifically earmarked for equipment.
entries.meaning: Narrows a general statement down to the exact case, and it is the one word in this family that takes either a full clause or a bare phrase after it. Namely closes a set; specifically sharpens a description — and where i.e. restates the same thing in other terms, specifically moves one step down in generality.
examples: The audit found problems; specifically, four invoices had no matching purchase order.
Attendance is down. Specifically, weeknight showings have lost a third of their audience.
She objected to one line, specifically, the clause about weekend hours.
Specifically, the ordinance bars parking on the north side between two and six.
The room was built specifically for recording. (manner adverb — "expressly," not a connector)

entries.clause: No clause of its own — a comment adverbial narrowing what follows to its exact, technical truth. Grammatically a fronted participial phrase, and nothing in the sentence has to be doing the speaking.
entries.pattern: Strictly speaking, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [be], strictly speaking, [complement]. · [Independent clause], strictly speaking.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, commas on both sides in the middle, comma before it at the end. It joins no clauses on its own, so where two independent clauses meet the usual semicolon or period is still required.
entries.meaning: Signals that what follows is true by the exact definition, and usually that ordinary usage says otherwise: Strictly speaking, a tomato is a fruit. Its opposites are generally speaking and broadly speaking, and its constant companion is a mild pedantry the listener did not ask for.
examples: Strictly speaking, the building is in the township, not the city.
She is, strictly speaking, an independent contractor rather than an employee.
Strictly speaking, none of this is confidential, but I'd keep it to yourself.
A koala isn't a bear, strictly speaking.
Strictly speaking, the deadline is Friday; in practice, nobody reads them until Monday.

entries.clause: Independent clause or phrase — adverbial link of restatement and specification
entries.pattern: [clause], that is, [restatement]. · [Independent clause]. That is, [independent clause]. · [noun phrase] — that is, [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma, dash, or period before it, comma after it; commas on both sides when it sits inside a clause. Never a bare comma joining two independent clauses — use a period or semicolon there.
variants: or used appositively (the coda, or final section)
entries.meaning: Restates what came before in a more exact form, narrowing rather than paraphrasing. It sits between its two neighbors: in other words rewrites the whole idea in plainer language, while namely identifies the members of a set.
examples: We'll meet on the first Tuesday, that is, the seventh.
The offer applies to residents — that is, anyone who has lived here six months.
She's a stringer; that is, she's paid per story rather than by salary.
That is, no one had checked whether the permit was still valid.
He was let go for cause, that is to say, for cause the company never described.

entries.clause: A continuative relative clause that restates the whole clause before it. Because the which needs an antecedent in the same sentence, it cannot open one in edited prose — though writers break that rule for effect.
entries.pattern: [Independent clause], which is to say, [restatement]. · [Independent clause] — which is to say, [restatement]. · [noun phrase], which is to say [noun phrase], [continuation].
entries.punctuation: A comma or dash before it — this is one of the few restatement connectors that takes a comma rather than a semicolon, because the relative pronoun subordinates what follows. The comma after it is optional and usually dropped before a short phrase.
entries.meaning: Restates the preceding clause in sharper or franker terms, generally to expose what it really amounts to. Its relative-clause grammar is the practical difference from in other words: it attaches across a comma where in other words would demand a semicolon or a period.
examples: The position was eliminated, which is to say he was fired.
The fund is self-insured, which is to say the county pays every claim out of the general budget.
They asked for volunteers — which is to say, they asked us.
The trial ended in a hung jury, which is to say nothing was decided at all.
The house is a fixer-upper, which is to say the floors are gone.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of justification. In final position, a different sense: "contrary to expectation."
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; after all, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. After all, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] after all. ("contrary to expectation")
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it in front position. In the "contrary to expectation" sense it closes the clause and takes no comma before it — She came after all, not She came, after all.
entries.meaning: Two distinct jobs, and position tells you which one you have. As a connector it supplies a reason the hearer is expected to accept already: Don't be hard on him; after all, he's twelve. At the end of a clause it reports that the expected thing failed to happen: The flight wasn't canceled after all.
examples: Let him sleep in; after all, it's Saturday.
Nobody was surprised — she'd been training for a year, after all.
After all, we did agree to split the cost down the middle.
The flight wasn't canceled after all. (the "contrary to expectation" sense)
It turned out they had a table for us after all.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of emphatic correction or confirmation
entries.pattern: As a matter of fact, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; as a matter of fact, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [be/auxiliary], as a matter of fact, [complement]. · [Independent clause], as a matter of fact.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, commas on both sides in the middle, comma before it at the end; a semicolon or period where two independent clauses meet — a bare comma there is a comma splice.
variants: matter of fact (informal and comma-free: matter of fact, I did)
entries.meaning: Introduces a fact that contradicts, corrects, or one-ups what the listener has just assumed, and it is markedly more combative than plain in fact because the phrase itself announces that a correction is coming. In American conversation it very often prefaces a small triumph: As a matter of fact, I have.
examples: As a matter of fact, I was just about to call you.
"You've never been to Texas." "As a matter of fact, I lived in Austin for two years."
The tenants were never notified; as a matter of fact, the notice went to the wrong address.
She isn't new here, as a matter of fact — she trained everyone in the room.
As a matter of fact, the same question came up at the last meeting.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link introducing a fact learned after the event, usually one that upsets the expectation just described
entries.pattern: As it turns out, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; as it turns out, [independent clause]. · [Subject], as it turns out, [predicate]. · [Independent clause], as it turns out.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, commas on both sides in the middle, comma before it at the end. Between two independent clauses a semicolon or period is required — a bare comma is a comma splice.
variants: as it happens (a coincidence rather than a discovery)
sure enough (when the expectation was confirmed instead of upset)
entries.meaning: Reports what was learned later, and almost always marks a reversal: the thing everyone assumed turns out to be wrong. As it happens is the milder cousin, flagging a lucky coincidence rather than a correction, and it turns out is the same connector with the subordinator dropped.
examples: As it turns out, the check had cleared two days before the letter went out.
We packed for rain. As it turns out, it was eighty degrees all week.
The building was condemned in 1998; as it turns out, three families were still living in it.
Her grandfather, as it turns out, had worked in the same plant.
As it happens, I have a copy in the car.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of emphasis marking the following point as the decisive one. Also an ordinary degree adverb inside the clause (crucially dependent on the discount rate), which takes no commas.
entries.pattern: Crucially, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; crucially, [independent clause]. · [Subject], crucially, [predicate]. · [Independent clause], and crucially, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [be] crucially [adjective]. (degree adverb — no commas)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle; a semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses. Without the commas it modifies the adjective beside it rather than the whole sentence.
entries.meaning: Flags the sentence it opens as the one the argument turns on — the workhorse of research abstracts and analytical journalism. It ranks a point rather than merely adding one, which is what separates it from moreover.
examples: Crucially, the second trial included patients over seventy-five.
The bill passed the House; crucially, it did so without a single amendment.
The lease runs another eight years and, crucially, cannot be assigned.
Crucially, no one has explained where the money came from.
The outcome is crucially dependent on the discount rate. (degree adverb — not a connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of emphasis marking the following statement as significant. Also a manner adverb meaning "with a self-important air" (he nodded importantly), a wholly different word.
entries.pattern: Importantly, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; importantly, [independent clause]. · [Subject], importantly, [predicate]. · [Subject] [verb] importantly. (manner adverb — "pompously," no commas)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle; a semicolon or period before it when two independent clauses are joined. The commas are what keep it from being read as manner.
entries.meaning: Marks its sentence as one of the significant ones without ranking it against anything in particular, where more importantly explicitly outranks the point before it. Traditionalists once objected that the word should only mean "in an important manner," but the sentence-adverb use has long since won.
examples: Importantly, the study was funded by the state rather than by the manufacturer.
The building passed inspection; importantly, the sprinkler system was tested under load.
The settlement pays the back wages and, importantly, admits no wrongdoing.
Importantly, none of this was disclosed to the buyers.
He cleared his throat and nodded importantly. (manner adverb — "with a self-important air")

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of emphasis or correction
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; in fact, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. In fact, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] — in fact, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [be/auxiliary], in fact, [complement].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon, period, or dash before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle.
entries.meaning: Introduces something stronger, more surprising, or flatly corrective of what the listener assumed. Compare indeed, which mostly confirms and intensifies: in fact is the word you reach for when the truth turns out to be different from the expectation.
examples: He said he'd never met her; in fact, they had worked together for three years.
The repair isn't difficult. In fact, you can do it with a screwdriver.
She wasn't annoyed — in fact, she seemed relieved.
The building is, in fact, older than the town charter.
As a matter of fact, I was just about to call you.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of emphatic confirmation
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; indeed, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Indeed, [independent clause]. · [adjective] — indeed, [stronger adjective]. · [phrase], indeed [stronger phrase], [continuation]. · Indeed [subject] [verb]. (integrated emphasizer — no comma) · "Indeed." (as a full reply)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas or dashes on both sides when it introduces an intensified restatement. As a reply token or an integrated emphasizer it takes no comma at all: Indeed it was.
variants: quite so (both dated or British-flavored in American speech)
entries.meaning: Confirms the previous statement and then pushes it further — "yes, and more so." Unlike in fact, it rarely corrects anything; it doubles down. It also serves as a one-word agreement token in formal speech.
examples: The book is long; indeed, it runs to nine hundred pages.
She was qualified — indeed, overqualified.
Indeed, the committee had warned about exactly this back in March.
"That was quite a storm." "Indeed it was."
The delay was costly, indeed ruinous, for the smaller vendors.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of addition that ranks the new point above the last
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; more importantly, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. More importantly, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], and more importantly, [independent clause]. · [Subject], more importantly, [predicate].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice unless and carries the join — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle.
variants: most importantly (for the last and greatest item in a list)
more important / most important (the older adjectival forms, still preferred by some editors)
entries.meaning: Adds a point and claims it outweighs the one before it — moreover with an explicit ranking. Use more importantly when two things are being compared and most importantly when you are topping off a list of three or more; the older more important (short for "what is more important") is equally correct, and the quarrel between the forms is now a matter of ear.
examples: The repair is cheap and, more importantly, it can be done today.
She knows the statute; more importantly, she knows the judge who wrote it.
More importantly, no one has asked the residents what they want.
The plan saves money. Most importantly, it keeps the clinic open.
Most important, the agency never published the data it relied on. (the older adjectival form)

entries.clause: No clause of its own — it introduces a stronger word or phrase that replaces the one just used. Also the archaic negative reply nay ("no"), which survives in recorded voice votes (the ayes and the nays).
entries.pattern: [phrase], nay, [stronger phrase]. · [adjective] — nay, [stronger adjective]. · [Independent clause]; nay, [stronger independent clause]. · "Nay," [reported speech]. (archaic "no")
entries.punctuation: Commas or dashes on both sides. Between two full independent clauses a semicolon before it is the usual choice; a comma alone there is a splice, exactly as with indeed.
entries.meaning: Corrects upward: it withdraws the word just used in favor of a stronger one — difficult, nay, impossible. In American English it survives only in deliberately elevated or jokey writing, in period fiction, and in the voice-vote formula the nays have it; anywhere else indeed or or rather is the living form.
examples: The task would be difficult, nay, impossible.
He was a rival, nay, an enemy, from the day they met.
"Nay, my lord, I know not what you mean." (period diction — the archaic "no")
The proposal is unwise — nay, reckless — and the council should reject it out of hand.
The clerk called the roll, and the nays carried the day. (the noun — a negative vote)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of concession or shared assumption. Also a standalone reply token ("Of course.") and, uncommaed, an integrated emphasizer inside the clause.
entries.pattern: Of course, [independent clause], but [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; of course, [independent clause]. · [Subject], of course, [predicate]. · [Subject] [verb], of course. · Of course [subject] [verb]. (integrated emphasizer — no comma) · "Of course." (as a full reply)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, commas on both sides in the middle, comma before it at the end. When two independent clauses are joined, a semicolon or period comes first — never a bare comma. The comma drops when of course is fully integrated into the clause as an emphasizer rather than set off as an aside: Of course the store was closed.
entries.meaning: Marks what follows as something everyone already knows or would expect — very often to concede a point before turning against it: Of course, the data is three years old, but the pattern holds. Watch the tone: attached to something the listener genuinely did not know, it reads as condescending.
examples: Of course, the estimate assumes nothing goes wrong.
She's the most experienced person in the room, of course.
Of course the store was closed by the time we got there.
The plan will cost money; of course, so will doing nothing.
"Can I borrow your charger?" "Of course."

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link confirming that what was expected or predicted did in fact happen
entries.pattern: Sure enough, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], and sure enough, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Sure enough, [independent clause]. · [Subject], sure enough, [predicate].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle; a period or semicolon before it unless and carries the join. Fast narrative often drops the comma after it (and sure enough it rained), which is standard in fiction and dialogue.
entries.meaning: Confirms a prediction, usually one that somebody made out loud a moment earlier: the storyteller's payoff word. It is the mirror image of as it turns out, which reports that the expectation was wrong.
examples: He said the transmission would go before winter, and sure enough, it did.
Sure enough, the flight was delayed again.
She told us to bring cash. Sure enough, the card reader was broken.
I checked the attic and, sure enough, there was the missing box.
The forecast called for ice; sure enough, school was canceled by six.

entries.clause: No clause of its own — a comment adverbial prefacing the speaker's frank opinion. Grammatically an infinitive phrase with no subject, held in place by convention rather than by grammar.
entries.pattern: To be honest, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], to be honest. · [Subject], to be honest, [predicate]. · To tell the truth, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, comma before it at the end, commas on both sides in the middle. It never joins two independent clauses by itself; a period or semicolon does that work.
entries.meaning: Warns that a candid and usually unflattering opinion is coming — and, by implication, that the speaker has been holding it back. To tell the truth is the same move in slightly older clothing and truth be told is the literary version; overused, all three read as filler rather than as candor.
examples: To be honest, I'd rather stay home.
The second half was a slog, to be honest.
To tell the truth, nobody on the committee had read the whole thing.
She is, to be honest, the only reason the department still functions.
To be honest, I never expected them to call back.

entries.clause: No clause of its own — a comment adverbial prefacing an admission. The verb is a fossilized subjunctive with its subject in front of it (truth be told, never the truth is told), which is why the phrase cannot be reworded.
entries.pattern: Truth be told, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], truth be told. · [Subject], truth be told, [predicate]. · If truth be told, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, comma before it at the end, commas on both sides in the middle. A semicolon or period still does the work of joining two independent clauses.
entries.meaning: Introduces something the speaker has been politely leaving out — a confession delivered with a slightly literary flourish. It is more written than to be honest, and it turns up constantly in memoir, sports columns, and obituaries.
examples: Truth be told, the house had never been worth what they paid for it.
He enjoyed the attention, truth be told.
Truth be told, none of us thought the team would make it past October.
She was, truth be told, relieved when the store finally closed.
Truth be told, I'd forgotten the meeting entirely until the reminder came through.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of summation (a net verdict)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. All in all, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; all in all, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it. Front position only.
entries.meaning: Delivers the net verdict after the details have been weighed — the everyday summing-up phrase of reviews and travel stories. It reports a judgment, where in short compresses information and in conclusion announces the end of a formal text.
examples: The flights were late and it rained twice. All in all, though, a good trip.
All in all, I'd rather have the older model.
There were a few rough edges; all in all, the show worked.
Overall, the program has done what it promised.
All things considered, we came out ahead.

entries.clause: No clause of its own — a nominative absolute phrase delivering a net judgment once everything on both sides has been weighed
entries.pattern: All things considered, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], all things considered. · [Subject] [be], all things considered, [complement].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, comma before it at the end, commas on both sides in the middle; a period or semicolon where two independent clauses meet.
entries.meaning: Announces a verdict reached after weighing the bad against the good, and it almost always concedes that there was something on the other side of the scale. All in all sums an experience up; all things considered judges it, often with the sense "given how it could have gone."
examples: All things considered, we came out ahead.
The car needs tires, but all things considered, it was a good buy.
She handled the interview well, all things considered.
All things considered, the district would rather settle than go to trial.
It was, all things considered, the least bad option on the table.
related: at the end of the day

entries.term: at the end of the day
entries.respell: ut thee END uv thuh DAY
entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of final judgment ("when everything else has been set aside"). Also a literal time adverbial (at the end of the day, lock the register), which is not a connector.
entries.pattern: At the end of the day, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; at the end of the day, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], at the end of the day. · [Independent clause] at the end of the day.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position and a comma before it at the end; a period or semicolon between two independent clauses. The literal time sense takes the same commas, so only the meaning tells the two apart.
variants: when all is said and done
entries.meaning: Sweeps the details aside and states what the speaker thinks really governs — the reflex phrase of coaches, executives, and pundits, and one of the most complained-about clichés in American English. In writing, ultimately or in the end says the same thing in three fewer words.
examples: At the end of the day, the voters decide.
We can argue about the design; at the end of the day, we have to ship something.
At the end of the day, it's a business, not a family.
He's difficult to work with, but at the end of the day he delivers.
At the end of the day, count the drawer and lock the safe. (literal time adverbial — not a connector)
related: when all is said and done

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of generalization ("with exceptions allowed for")
entries.pattern: By and large, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; by and large, [independent clause]. · [Subject], by and large, [predicate]. · [Independent clause], by and large.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, commas on both sides in the middle, comma before it at the end; a semicolon or period between two independent clauses.
entries.meaning: Concedes exceptions while asserting the general rule — closer to "mostly, though not always" than to "always." The phrase comes from sailing, where by and large named two ways of taking the wind, which is why its parts cannot be dropped or reordered.
examples: By and large, the tenants have been patient about the noise.
The buses run on time, by and large.
By and large, the changes were cosmetic.
Rural counties, by and large, lost population over the decade.
The reviews were mixed, but by and large audiences liked it.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of generalization stating that the claim holds for most of the cases
entries.pattern: For the most part, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; for the most part, [independent clause]. · [Subject], for the most part, [predicate]. · [Independent clause] for the most part.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle; at the end of a clause it usually runs on with no comma at all (the roads stayed clear for the most part). A semicolon or period is still required between two independent clauses.
entries.meaning: Says the statement covers most of the cases and quietly admits that it does not cover all of them. It is the most countable of the generalizers — it points at a proportion, where by and large points at an overall impression.
examples: For the most part, the crew had worked together for years.
The complaints, for the most part, were about parking.
Snow held off until midnight; for the most part, the roads stayed clear.
For the most part, we agree about what has to happen next.
She writes her own material for the most part.

entries.clause: No clause of its own — a comment adverbial announcing that what follows is a generalization. Like strictly speaking, it is a fronted participial phrase with nobody doing the speaking.
entries.pattern: Generally speaking, [independent clause]. · [Subject], generally speaking, [predicate]. · [Independent clause], generally speaking.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, commas on both sides in the middle, comma before it at the end. It joins no clauses on its own; a period or semicolon does that.
entries.meaning: Warns the listener not to press the statement too hard, because exceptions exist. Its exact opposite is strictly speaking, and the two often appear a sentence apart when a speaker is drawing the line between the usual case and the technical one.
examples: Generally speaking, the older machines are easier to repair.
Juries, generally speaking, are more skeptical than lawyers expect.
Generally speaking, you want the permit before you pour the slab.
The fee is refundable, generally speaking, up to thirty days out.
Generally speaking, that neighborhood floods twice a decade.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of closure
entries.pattern: In conclusion, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. In conclusion, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Period before it — it opens the final paragraph or the final sentence — and a comma after it. Front position only.
entries.meaning: Announces the closing section of a speech, essay, or formal report. Use it once, at the actual end. In anything shorter than a few pages it reads as padding, and American editors routinely cut it.
examples: In conclusion, the evidence supports the second hypothesis.
In conclusion, I want to thank the families who took part in this study.
The findings are mixed. In conclusion, the authors recommend a larger trial.
In closing, let me return to the question we started with.
In conclusion, the committee finds no basis for the complaint.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of summation ("in short, to conclude")
entries.pattern: In fine, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; in fine, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. In fine, [independent clause]. · [series], and, in fine, [last item].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it, and a period or semicolon before it — a bare comma joining two independent clauses is a comma splice. Front position is the normal placement.
entries.meaning: From Latin in fine, "at the end" — the eighteenth- and nineteenth-century way of saying in short. An American meets it in Johnson, Burke, the Federalist Papers, and older sermons; written today it is either a period effect or a confusion with the unrelated legal citation in fine ("at the end of the page cited").
examples: In fine, the whole scheme rested on credit that no one had troubled to verify.
He was learned, industrious, and honest; in fine, a man made for the work.
In fine, we must either enlarge the union or dissolve it.
The evidence was circumstantial, contradictory, and, in fine, worthless.
In fine, there is no remedy but patience.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of generalization. Also a postmodifier attached directly to a noun phrase (readers in general), which takes no commas.
entries.pattern: In general, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; in general, [independent clause]. · [Subject], in general, [predicate]. · [Noun phrase] in general [verb phrase]. (postmodifier — no commas)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle; a semicolon or period between two independent clauses. Attached to a noun it takes none at all: readers in general don't notice.
entries.meaning: States the ordinary case and leaves room for exceptions, without the folksiness of by and large or the proportion-counting of for the most part. Note the second job: pinned to a noun it means "taken as a whole," and the missing commas are the only signal.
examples: In general, the fee is waived for first-time applicants.
Winters here are, in general, milder than people expect.
In general, we don't take appointments after four.
The report says little about hospitals in general and nothing about rural ones. (postmodifier — no commas)
In general, the older the roof, the higher the premium.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of summation (compression)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. In short, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; in short, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — and a comma after it. Front position only.
entries.meaning: Compresses everything just laid out into a single sentence. Where in conclusion signals structure — this is the end — in short signals compression, and it can appear anywhere in a text, including in the middle of an argument.
examples: The engine is shot, the frame is bent, the title is missing. In short, it's junk.
In short, we cannot afford both.
He wanted more money, fewer hours, and a new title; in short, a different job.
Long story short, we ended up driving back at two in the morning.
In sum, the policy achieved none of its stated goals.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of final judgment
entries.pattern: In the final analysis, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; in the final analysis, [independent clause]. · [Subject], in the final analysis, [predicate].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle; a semicolon or period between two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice.
variants: when all is said and done
at the end of the day (the spoken equivalent)
entries.meaning: The formal register's version of at the end of the day: it sets the details aside and names what finally decides the question. Editors treat it as padding whenever it opens a sentence that would stand perfectly well without it.
examples: In the final analysis, the case turned on a single unsigned memo.
The reforms were popular; in the final analysis, they changed almost nothing.
Responsibility, in the final analysis, rests with the board that approved the loan.
In the final analysis, the choice is between raising rates and closing branches.
In the last analysis, no treaty binds a government that refuses to be bound.
related: at the end of the day
when all is said and done

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of generalization ("for the most part")
entries.pattern: In the main, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; in the main, [independent clause]. · [Subject], in the main, [predicate]. · [Independent clause] in the main.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle; a semicolon or period between two independent clauses. At the end of a clause it often runs on without a comma.
entries.meaning: A bookish, slightly old-fashioned for the most part, at home in reviews, editorials, and formal reports. American readers register it as literary; in speech, mostly and by and large have taken the job over.
examples: In the main, the objections were procedural rather than substantive.
The translation is, in the main, faithful to the original.
Attendance held up in the main, though the Sunday matinees suffered.
In the main, the state's schools are funded by property taxes.
Her account agrees, in the main, with what the other witnesses described.

entries.clause: No clause of its own — an elliptical absolute phrase, clipped from to make a long story short, announcing that the speaker is skipping to the outcome
entries.pattern: Long story short, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Long story short, [independent clause]. · To make a long story short, [independent clause]. (the full form)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it, and a period before it, since it opens a new sentence. Front position only — it cannot close a clause or sit in the middle of one.
variants: to make a long story short
to cut a long story short (British)
entries.meaning: The storyteller's fast-forward: it skips the middle of the anecdote and delivers the result. It is purely conversational — a written summary uses in short — and it is very often deployed after the story has already gone on too long.
examples: Long story short, we ended up driving back at two in the morning.
The tow truck never came. Long story short, we slept in the car.
Long story short, she got the job.
To make a long story short, the permit had been in the wrong name the whole time.
Long story short, don't lend him anything you want back.
related: at the end of the day

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of generalized summation ("taking everything together")
entries.pattern: On the whole, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; on the whole, [independent clause]. · [Subject], on the whole, [predicate]. · [Independent clause], on the whole.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, commas on both sides in the middle, comma before it at the end; a semicolon or period between two independent clauses.
entries.meaning: Weighs the whole of something and reports where the balance falls — halfway between the generalizing by and large and the summing-up all in all. It is the mildest way in English to say the good outweighed the bad without denying that there was bad.
examples: On the whole, the season went better than anyone expected.
The reviews were kind, on the whole.
On the whole, I'd rather deal with the county than with the city.
The changes have, on the whole, made the form harder to read.
It was a difficult year; on the whole, though, the shop is stronger than it was.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of summation
entries.pattern: To sum up, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. To sum up, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Period before it, comma after it. Front position only.
entries.meaning: Introduces a restatement of the main points, typically near the close of a talk or a report. Because it is an infinitive phrase, the clause that follows needs a subject that can plausibly do the summing — To sum up, we recommend… works; To sum up, the results were poor is technically a dangler, though it passes unremarked in speech.
examples: To sum up, we recommend replacing the system rather than repairing it.
To sum up, three things went wrong and all three were preventable.
To summarize, the drug is safe but no more effective than aspirin.
To recap, we meet at eight, we leave at nine, and we're back by six.
In summary, the department met two of its four targets.

entries.term: when all is said and done
entries.respell: wen awl iz sed und DUN
entries.type: conjunctive adverb (phrasal — a fixed subordinate clause)
entries.clause: Formally a subordinate when clause, but frozen as a summing-up connective: nothing in the main clause has to be simultaneous with any saying or doing
entries.pattern: When all is said and done, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] when all is said and done. · [Subject], when all is said and done, [predicate].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position; the comma before it at the end is optional, as with any trailing adverbial clause. Because it is a subordinate clause rather than a bare adverb, it can attach with a comma where a conjunctive adverb would need a semicolon.
variants: at the end of the day
when it comes down to it
entries.meaning: Sets the arguing aside and names the thing that finally counts. It is the same move as at the end of the day with an older and more sententious ring, and it carries the same risk of sounding like filler.
examples: When all is said and done, the house is still standing.
He'll complain for a week, but when all is said and done he'll sign it.
When all is said and done, the strike cost both sides more than the raise was worth.
The awards are nice; when all is said and done, though, the work is what lasts.
When all is said and done, we are talking about eleven dollars a month.
related: at the end of the day

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of alternative
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; alternatively, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Alternatively, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [modal], alternatively, [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle.
entries.meaning: Offers a second option as a whole sentence — the adverb answering to or. Or joins two elements inside one sentence; alternatively starts a new one, which is why instructions and proposals lean on it so heavily.
examples: You can file online; alternatively, you can mail the form to the county office.
We could rent a van. Alternatively, we could make two trips.
Alternatively, the committee may postpone the vote until spring.
Bake for forty minutes or, alternatively, simmer the whole thing on the stove.
Pay the balance in full; alternatively, set up a twelve-month plan.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of dismissal, or a discourse marker returning to the main topic
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. Anyway, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; anyway, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] anyway. · [Independent clause], but [independent clause] anyway.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position; no comma before it in final position (I worried anyway). Period or semicolon before it when it opens a new independent clause — a bare comma there is a comma splice.
variants: anyhow (equally standard, a little more casual)
anyways (nonstandard but common in casual American speech)
any way (two words = "by any method" — a different phrase entirely)
entries.meaning: Three conversational jobs: returning to the main thread after a digression (Anyway, where was I?), dismissing what was just said as not changing anything (It's expensive. I'm buying it anyway), and closing a topic or a phone call (Anyway, I should let you go). Written nevertheless covers only the middle one.
examples: Anyway, that's how we ended up in Tulsa.
He told me not to worry about it. I worried anyway.
The store was closing, but they let us in anyway.
Anyway, I should let you go — it's late there.
"Anyhow," she said, "the roof still leaks."
It's probably closed by now; anyway, we don't need much.

entries.clause: No clause of its own — a fronted topic-shifting preposition taking a noun phrase or a gerund, which then becomes what the sentence is about
entries.pattern: As for [noun phrase], [independent clause]. · As for [gerund phrase], [independent clause]. · As for [wh- clause], [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: A comma closes the fronted phrase and separates it from the clause that follows. No semicolon is involved, because what comes after as for is a phrase rather than a second independent clause.
entries.meaning: Turns the spotlight onto the next topic — usually one already on the table, and often with an edge: As for Dan, he can find his own ride. It differs from regarding by presupposing that the topic has come up already, and it very often prefaces a dismissal.
examples: As for the money, we'll settle up on Friday.
As for the roof, it can wait until spring.
She's taking the train. As for me, I'm driving.
As for whether he knew, nobody has been able to establish it.
As for renewing the lease, the owner hasn't returned a single call.

entries.clause: No clause of its own — a topic-marking preposition taking a noun phrase. Note the fixed -s: as regards, never as regard.
entries.pattern: As regards [noun phrase], [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] as regards [noun phrase]. · [Subject] [be] silent as regards [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: A comma closes the phrase when it is fronted; no comma when it sits inside the predicate (silent as regards damages). No semicolon, since a noun phrase follows it.
entries.meaning: The bureaucratic topic-marker of reports, memoranda, and older business correspondence. American usage guides — Fowler and Garner among them — treat this whole family as flabby, and about, on, or for will usually replace it without any loss.
examples: As regards the second invoice, the department has no record of receiving it.
The contract is silent as regards renewal.
As regards staffing, the clinic has been two nurses short since June.
Nothing has changed as regards our position on the easement.
As regards the timeline, we expect a decision before the end of the quarter.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (phrasal — a fixed clause-final tag)
entries.clause: No clause of its own — it closes a disjunction and tells the reader that whichever of the listed alternatives actually applies is the one meant
entries.pattern: [alternative] or [alternative], as the case may be. · [Independent clause] [alternative] or [alternative], as the case may be, [continuation]. · [Noun phrase], or [noun phrase] as the case may be, [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: A comma before it always, and a second comma after it when the sentence continues. It sits at the end of the disjunction it closes and never at the head of a sentence.
variants: respectively (a different job — it pairs listed items in order)
entries.meaning: A drafter's device for writing one sentence that covers several situations at once: the reader supplies whichever alternative fits the facts. It belongs to contracts, statutes, and forms, and respectively is not a synonym, since that word matches items one-to-one rather than selecting among them.
examples: The notice shall be delivered to the Buyer or the Seller, as the case may be.
Payment is due within thirty days of the invoice or the delivery date, as the case may be.
The application must be signed by the applicant or the applicant's guardian, as the case may be, before it is filed.
Interest accrues at the contract rate or the statutory rate, as the case may be.
The plaintiff, or the defendant as the case may be, bears the cost of the transcript.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of dismissal (setting aside uncertainty)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. At any rate, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; at any rate, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], at any rate.
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and a comma before it at the end (that's what he told me, at any rate).
entries.meaning: Sets aside the uncertainty of what was just said and moves to what is certain: "whatever the truth of that, here is what holds." It sits closer to hedging than in any case does — it very often follows a correction or a qualification the speaker has just made about their own words.
examples: The meeting may be moved; at any rate, don't book anything for Thursday.
I think he said Tuesday. At any rate, it was early in the week.
She never confirmed it — that was the impression, at any rate.
At any rate, we can't do anything until the permit comes through.
The numbers may be off, but the direction is right, at any rate.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of digression. Also a literal prepositional phrase in older English (they met him by the way, "along the road"), which is not a connector.
entries.pattern: By the way, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; by the way, [independent clause]. · [Subject], by the way, [predicate]. · [Independent clause], by the way.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, commas on both sides in the middle, comma before it at the end; a semicolon or period between two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice.
entries.meaning: Marks what follows as a side remark — and, like incidentally, it is regularly used for the most important thing in the message, dropped in as though it were an afterthought. It is the standard spoken form; incidentally is what the same sentence wears in print.
examples: By the way, did the package ever show up?
The office is closed Monday. By the way, so is the pharmacy.
Your brother called, by the way.
By the way, we're going to need another chair.
The car, by the way, has been making that noise since March.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (phrasal — a fixed infinitival tag)
entries.clause: No clause of its own — it flags what follows as something that occurred to the speaker in the act of speaking
entries.pattern: Come to think of it, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] — come to think of it, [independent clause]. · [Subject], come to think of it, [predicate]. · [Independent clause], come to think of it.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, commas or dashes on both sides in the middle, comma before it at the end; a period, dash, or semicolon where two independent clauses meet.
variants: now that I think about it
on second thought (a change of mind rather than a new thought)
entries.meaning: Marks a realization arriving mid-conversation: the speaker did not plan to say this. It differs from on second thought, which revises a decision already announced, and from incidentally, which flags a digression the speaker had ready.
examples: Come to think of it, I never did get that deposit back.
She hasn't been to a meeting since March — come to think of it, neither has he.
Come to think of it, the same thing happened last winter.
There's a spare key in the garage, come to think of it.
Come to think of it, he never actually said yes.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link that disposes of everything not already dealt with ("as for the remainder")
entries.pattern: For the rest, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; for the rest, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. For the rest, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, with a semicolon or period before it when two independent clauses are joined — a bare comma there is a comma splice. Front position is the normal placement.
entries.meaning: Sweeps up whatever the writer has not addressed and characterizes it in one stroke — a device of nineteenth-century narration and formal review writing. An American reader meets it in translated fiction and older criticism; otherwise or in other respects is the current phrasing.
examples: The kitchen had been rebuilt. For the rest, the house was as their grandfather left it.
Two chapters are new; for the rest, the book is unchanged from the 1951 edition.
For the rest, the town offered nothing that would keep a young man in it.
He answered the first question fully. For the rest, he referred the committee to his written statement.
The soup was excellent; for the rest, the meal was forgettable.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of dismissal (true under every alternative)
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. In any case, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; in any case, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], in any case.
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and a comma before it at the end.
entries.meaning: Declares that what follows is true no matter which of the possibilities just raised turns out to be right. It is a shade more decisive than at any rate: it does not hedge, it closes the branch.
examples: She may not even want the job; in any case, we should interview two more people.
The forecast is uncertain. In any case, bring a jacket.
In any case, the deadline hasn't changed.
He might resign, or he might be pushed out; the seat opens in June, in any case.
In any event, the university will honor the original offer.
