entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of dismissal: what follows holds no matter which of the possibilities just raised turns out to be true
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]. In any event, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; in any event, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], in any event. · [Subject], in any event, [predicate].
entries.punctuation: Period or semicolon before it — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and a comma before it at the end.
entries.meaning: The formal twin of in any case, and the standard form in legal writing, where it introduces the argument that wins even if the previous one loses: In any event, the claim is time-barred. In ordinary speech it sounds stiff, and anyway does the work.
examples: The letter may never have been sent; in any event, it was never received.
In any event, the university will honor the original offer.
The statute does not apply to volunteers. In any event, the plaintiff was not a volunteer.
We can argue about the numbers, but the plant closes in June, in any event.
In any event, nobody disputes that the money was paid.

entries.register: formal, legal (commoner in British than American drafting)
entries.clause: No clause of its own — a topic-marking preposition taking a noun phrase, most often naming what a payment, claim, or obligation relates to
entries.pattern: [Independent clause] in respect of [noun phrase]. · In respect of [noun phrase], [independent clause]. · [amount] payable in respect of [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: No commas inside the predicate; a comma closes the phrase when it is fronted. No semicolon, since a noun phrase follows it.
entries.meaning: Contract and tax language for "relating to," normally attached to money: amounts payable in respect of the period ending June 30. American drafters reach for with respect to far more often, and outside a legal instrument a plain for or on is better in nearly every case.
examples: No further sums are payable in respect of the 2023 tax year.
In respect of the disputed invoices, the parties have agreed to mediate.
The company has made no provision in respect of the pending claims.
Interest accrues in respect of each day the balance remains outstanding.
In respect of the second property, title has not yet been registered.

entries.clause: No clause of its own — a preposition taking a noun phrase or gerund and naming the dimension along which a claim is being measured
entries.pattern: [Independent clause] in terms of [noun phrase]. · In terms of [noun phrase], [independent clause]. · [Subject] [verb] in terms of [gerund phrase].
entries.punctuation: A comma closes the phrase when it is fronted; no commas inside the predicate. It never takes a semicolon, because a noun phrase follows it rather than a clause.
entries.meaning: Properly, it names the units or the framework of a comparison: cheap in terms of fuel, expensive in terms of maintenance. In speech it has spread far past that job and now serves as an all-purpose topic marker (in terms of scheduling, we're fine), which is the use editors cut on sight.
examples: The plan is attractive in terms of cost and hopeless in terms of timing.
In terms of enrollment, the district has been flat for a decade.
Measured in terms of revenue rather than headcount, it is the larger company.
Results are usually reported in terms of deaths per hundred thousand.
In terms of what happens next, nobody has told us anything. (the vague topic-marker use — editors cut it)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link asserting that what follows bears on the matter just discussed
entries.pattern: In this connection, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; in this connection, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [auxiliary], in this connection, [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle; a semicolon or period between two independent clauses.
entries.meaning: The scholarly and diplomatic way of saying "and here is something that bears on that" — the ordinary furniture of UN documents, older monographs, and formal correspondence. It claims relevance rather than adding weight, which is what separates it from moreover.
examples: In this connection, the Committee recalls its earlier recommendation on detention conditions.
Two of the manuscripts are dated. In this connection, the watermark evidence becomes decisive.
In this connection, it should be noted that the author never visited the region.
The department has, in this connection, requested a further report from the inspector.
In this connection, the Board wishes to draw attention to the auditors' third finding.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link that limits a claim to one particular dimension of comparison
entries.pattern: In this respect, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; in this respect, [independent clause]. · [Subject] [be], in this respect, [complement]. · [Independent clause] in this respect.
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle; a semicolon or period between two independent clauses. At the end of a clause it usually runs on with no comma: the two cases differ in this respect.
entries.meaning: Restricts what follows to a single dimension, and so quietly concedes that the comparison might go the other way on some other dimension. In this connection claims relevance; in this respect draws a boundary around the claim.
examples: In this respect, the two agencies operate under identical rules.
Missouri was, in this respect, ahead of every state around it.
The new engine is quieter; in this respect, at least, the redesign succeeded.
The statutes differ in this respect: one requires notice and the other does not.
In this respect, the company's disclosures were no worse than its competitors'.

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of digression. Also a manner adverb meaning "by chance, as a side effect" (the drug was discovered incidentally), which sits in the predicate and takes no commas.
entries.pattern: Incidentally, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]; incidentally, [independent clause]. · [Subject], incidentally, [predicate]. · [Subject] [verb phrase] incidentally. (manner adverb — "by chance," no commas)
entries.punctuation: Semicolon or period before it when it links two independent clauses — a bare comma there is a comma splice — with a comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle. The commas are what mark it as a digression rather than a manner adverb.
variants: speaking of which (when the topic itself prompts the aside)
entries.meaning: Flags what follows as a remark off the main line of the argument. It is the written equivalent of by the way — and like by the way, it is routinely used for information the speaker considers anything but incidental.
examples: Incidentally, the same firm audited both companies.
Her father, incidentally, had held the same seat thirty years earlier.
The building is being sold; incidentally, the tenants weren't told until yesterday.
Incidentally, you still owe me twenty dollars.
By the way, did the package ever show up?
The compound was discovered incidentally, during a search for a better solvent. (manner adverb — "by chance," not a digression marker)

entries.clause: Independent clause or phrase — adverbial link that scales the previous claim back a step, "or at any rate"
entries.pattern: [Independent clause], leastways [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Leastways, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause], leastways [phrase].
entries.punctuation: Dialect writing gives it a bare comma before and none after, and that loose punctuation is part of the effect. By the standard rule the two independent clauses still need a period or semicolon between them.
entries.meaning: A regional variant of at least, used to walk a statement back a step — Appalachian, Ozark, and rural Southern speech, and a fixture of nineteenth-century American fiction. It is nonstandard: use it to render a voice, never in your own prose.
examples: Nobody's been up there in years — leastways nobody I know of.
He said he'd pay it back. Leastways, that's what I understood.
The well never went dry, leastwise not in my lifetime.
"She's gone to her sister's, leastways that's what the note said."
They don't run the ferry in winter, leastways not on weekdays.

entries.clause: Independent clause — a discourse-structuring link moving the listener to the next stage of an argument, a set of instructions, or a story. Distinct from the ordinary time adverb now ("at this moment"), which sits in the predicate and takes no commas.
entries.pattern: Now, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Now, [independent clause]. · Now [imperative]. · [Subject] [verb] now. (time adverb — "at this moment," no commas)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position, with a period or semicolon before it, since it opens a new sentence — a bare comma there is a comma splice. Speakers and recipe writers routinely drop that comma (Now add the garlic), and in instructions the comma-free form is standard.
entries.meaning: Not time at all: this now is the spoken paragraph break, moving the discussion to the next point (Now, the second question is harder) or softening a coming correction (Now, that's not quite what I said). Written next covers only the sequencing job; the corrective and throat-clearing jobs belong to now alone.
examples: Now, the second question is harder to answer.
We've settled the budget. Now, about the schedule.
Now, I'm not saying she was wrong.
Brown the onions. Now add the garlic and cook it a minute longer.
Now then, who wants to go first?
The office is closed now. (ordinary time adverb — not a connector)

entries.clause: Independent clause — adverbial link of dismissal: the outcome holds whichever of the possible routes turns out to be taken
entries.pattern: One way or another, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] one way or another. · [Subject] [modal], one way or another, [verb phrase]. · [Independent clause], one way or another, [continuation].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it in front position and commas on both sides in the middle; at the end of a clause it commonly takes no comma at all (we'll get there one way or another). Between two independent clauses, a period or semicolon.
variants: one way or the other (usually about a choice between two)
entries.meaning: Declares that the result is settled even though the means are not — often with a note of threat or grim determination. Either way looks back at two alternatives already named; one way or another leaves the alternatives unspecified.
examples: One way or another, the rent gets paid on the first.
We'll find out one way or another before the week is out.
One way or another, every one of those trees is coming down.
She was going to hear about it one way or another.
The dispute has to end, one way or another, before the season starts.

entries.clause: No clause of its own — a topic-linking tag whose which points back at the subject just raised. In the open form, speaking of takes a noun phrase of its own.
entries.pattern: Speaking of which, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] — speaking of which, [independent clause]. · Speaking of [noun phrase], [independent clause]. (the open form)
entries.punctuation: Comma after it, and a period or dash before it, since it opens its own sentence. The open form takes the comma that closes any fronted phrase: Speaking of Dan, has anyone heard from him?
entries.meaning: Takes the topic that just came up and uses it as the doorway to a related remark, so the digression arrives licensed rather than abrupt. Incidentally announces an unrelated aside; speaking of which claims the previous sentence handed it the subject.
examples: The tickets go on sale Friday. Speaking of which, do you still want two?
He's been in Chicago all month — speaking of which, did his flight ever get rebooked?
Speaking of which, the inspection is scheduled for Tuesday.
Speaking of the roof, the estimate came in this morning.
We were talking about the budget. Speaking of which, nobody has approved the travel line.

entries.clause: No clause of its own — a topic-marking preposition taking a noun phrase or gerund. Note the singular: with regard to, not with regards to, which belongs at the end of a letter.
entries.pattern: With regard to [noun phrase], [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] with regard to [noun phrase]. · [Subject] [verb phrase] with regard to [gerund phrase].
entries.punctuation: A comma closes the fronted phrase; no commas when it sits inside the predicate. No semicolon, since a noun phrase follows it.
entries.meaning: The letter-writer's topic marker: "on the subject of." With regards to — with the -s — is a common error borrowed from the sign-off best regards. American style guides rate the whole family as wordy, and about or on usually improves the sentence.
examples: With regard to your letter of March 4, the file has been reopened.
The board has taken no position with regard to the sale.
With regard to parking, the permit office opens at eight.
Nothing in the policy is specific with regard to remote work.
With regard to the second charge, the defendant has entered no plea.

entries.clause: No clause of its own — a topic-marking preposition taking a noun phrase. In mathematics and the sciences it carries a technical sense, "measured against, as the variable" (differentiate with respect to x), which is not a connector at all.
entries.pattern: With respect to [noun phrase], [independent clause]. · [Independent clause] with respect to [noun phrase]. · [Subject] [verb] with respect to [variable]. (technical sense)
entries.punctuation: A comma closes the fronted phrase; no commas inside the predicate. No semicolon, since what follows is a noun phrase rather than a clause.
entries.meaning: The standard American drafting phrase for "concerning, as applied to" — the workhorse of contracts, opinions, and technical writing, where its precision earns its length. In everyday prose it is padding; note the scientific use, though, where it names the variable of differentiation and cannot be replaced by about.
examples: The Seller makes no warranty with respect to the condition of the roof.
With respect to the third count, the motion is denied.
The company has no obligations with respect to employees hired after the closing.
Differentiate the function with respect to time. (the technical sense — not a connector)
With respect to the remaining items, we can take them up next week.
